subsubtopic: RELEASE OF U.S.S.R. POLITICAL PRISONERS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that pressures of world public opinion and intervention by governments, including that of the Soviet Union, requesting full amnesty and the release of political prisoners, have had positive results in Greece, Portugal, Chile and, most recently, in Cuba-with the release of over 3,000 political prisoners-and to promote further international cooperation and detente, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan):
That this House urge the government to make direct representation at the highest level to the government of the U.S.S.R. to grant full amnesty to all prisoners of conscience on its territory, as a gesture of good will, in compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the human rights provisions of the Helsinki Accords, assuring Canada's willingness to consider positively requests for admission to Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing necessity.
Considering that on November 8 last, as reported in Hansard on page 915, the Minister of Finance confirmed in the House that the inspector general of banks was conducting an inquiry on the part which chartered banks may have played in the devaluation of the Canadian dollar to make substantial profits; considering the fact also that chartered banks have announced record profits for the financial year ending on October 31 last, increasing by as much as 58.6 per cent in one case; in view of the fact finally that the dollar is falling lower from day to day, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House direct the Minister of Finance to table as soon as possible a report on the inquiry made by the superintendent of banks on the part which chartered banks may have played on the devaluation of the Canadian dollar.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter or urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
The Postmaster General is continuing the freeze on door-to-door delivery of mail in new suburbs in many cities across Canada which are feeling the pressure of a rapid increase in population, and this notwithstanding a continuing unemployment rate of close to one million Canadians. In view of the fact that many jobs are being eliminated by this continuing freeze, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling):
That the Post Office Department establish this traditional service, thereby providing Canadians with the quality of mail service to which they are entitled and that the money be made available by delaying the costly move to metric announced recently by the Postmaster General and by savings from the unemployment insurance fund.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: EXPLANATION FOR HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the jobless Figures released by Statistics Canada paint the rather gloomy picture of 977,000 Canadians unemployed, a substantial increase when you take into account the rate of hidden unemployment in the country, because using StatCan's own methodology we have a million and a quarter Canadians unemployed in this country.
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, given the minister's and the Prime Minister's propensity to paint such a rosy picture of the economy and of job creation prospects, if the minister could explain to the House and to the country why the jobless rate has increased this month by 120,000.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATION FOR HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if one compares the situation this year with last year, there is a decrease in unemployment in that last year we created more than 450,000 jobs from January to January. I think it is a very good result but it is not a satisfactory one. We are always working very hard to ensure that job creation will be better, but one must understand that the participation rate in Canada is very, very high. This month we attained a record high level in terms of the participation rate; in fact, from January to January there were 450,000 more Canadians at work.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATION FOR HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, given the minister's reply and his failure to explain why the jobless rate in the country is up by over 120,000, the forecast of the Conference Board in Canada that job creation this year will not exceed 197,000, and the economic forecasts of 4 per cent real growth, will the minister tell the House his latest estimate of job creation for 1979? I am sure the 1.25 million unemployed Canadians would like to know what the prospects are for this year.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATION FOR HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, traditionally, come January the number of unemployed is higher in Canada because of the particular working conditions in winter; there is nothing there to be excited about. I want to tell the hon. member that last August the Conference Board had predicted that the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment would reach 9 per cent in January and that this rate is now 8.1 per cent, which is better than was predicted.

subsubtopic: EXPLANATION FOR HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the forecast of the Minister of Finance is about as accurate as his forecasts of the rate of inflation which he has had to correct from time to time.
My supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. The industrial heartland of the country, the famous Golden Triangle, has the highest rate of
Oral Questions
urban unemployment in Canada, 13.6 per cent in the St. Catharines-Niagara region. The unemployment rate in the Atlantic provinces now is hovering around 13 per cent, 17.6 per cent in Newfoundland.
Given the minister's propensity to tell the unemployed youth of the Atlantic provinces to travel across the country, and that there is an unemployment rate of 13.6 per cent in the industrial heartland, where are the youth to go? Can the minister tell us where they are able to go to look for jobs?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Last October 26 the Quebec minister of state for economic development stated that, according to a study he made public, if no compensatory measures were taken by Ottawa the federal budget cuts would entail a loss of more than 18,000 jobs; since Statistics Canada has

February 6, 1979
Oral Questions
reported this morning that from last month up till today there has been an increase of 30,000 more jobless in Quebec, would the Minister of Finance not recognize today the validity of that study and say what compensatory measures he is prepared to bring before the Flouse?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when we announced our budget cuts last August it was to make sure that the Canadian economy would work in a more proper way and because it had then become necessary to reduce the public sector involvement in the economy. We have developed a policy which helps increase the private sector role in job creation. We have also decided that the public sector involvement could not get higher than its present level. The budget cuts we made in August have had a favourable effect on the Canadian economy since they have re-established a climate of confidence in Canada, and that is why we could report in January that the number of jobs in Canada in relation to January of last year was 450,000 new jobs added to the Canadian work force.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a supplementary.
It is all very well for the minister to remind us that jobs are obviously being created, but the fact remains that Statistics Canada has shown that the rate of unemployment has gone up. The Minister of Finance speaks of all provinces, in which of course we are interested, but I represent Quebec, and it is undergoing difficulties: it has been proved that it will pay dearly for the budgetary cuts. As the minister knows that province well, I am asking him whether he has compensatory measures to offer with a view to remedying that situation which in the last 30 days has grown to seemingly disastrous proportions, especially in the case of Quebec.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the budgetary cuts we made in August were made right across the board, the same all over Canada. If Quebec is experiencing particular difficulties at this time, much of it can be blamed on the provincial government policy that scares both capital and people away from Quebec; if Quebec offered much greater political stability than it does now, its economy would be much healthier.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on another supplementary. The minister claims that Quebec's policy is scaring capital away; how then can he explain the fact that, looking at the figures for last year, the province of Quebec had 6,000 fewer unemployed then than it has today, at this point in time?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: That may be true, but the hon. member should compare the present situation with what it was two years ago when Quebec had a federalist government.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO TAKE TO COMPENSATE FOR LOST JOBS IN QUEBEC
speechtext: No, they have been in power for two years!

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance regarding his own difficulties in forecasting, particularly with reference to the unemployment situation which, any way you look at it today, is bad in real numbers with more than one million unemployed.
At the House committee this morning, when dealing with the operations of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Bouey made specific reference to the fact that in dealing with job creation we must expand the economy, especially our exports. I should like to ask the minister whether the government now has any new measures, in the form of either fiscal or monetary policies, such as decreasing Canadian interest rates, in order to expand the Canadian economy and produce more jobs?

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, monetary policy has been established by the governor of the Bank and I have agreed with that. It is very important to maintain the flow of capital, and in order to maintain stability of our currency it is important that we have these interest rates. There is no discussion at this time between myself and the governor of the possibility of reducing interest rates in the immediate future.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext:
What the minister is saying, Mr. Speaker, is that the unemployment situation is going to get worse, not better. In this context I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
In order to decrease our serious unemployment level and to alleviate our balance of payments problem, the governor of the Bank of Canada agreed this morning with something we have been saying for months, namely, that we have to expand our trade. Bearing in mind that one of the major impediments to increasing our exports is the branch plant nature of so much of Canadian manufacturing, and in view of the fact that the minister said on Friday "our efforts to promote long-term sales are getting cut off by foreign-owned company policies", I would like to ask what specific steps the government is taking to stop branch plant companies from using Canadian-generated profits to drum up business for their parent companies either in the United States or in other foreign lands?
Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and
Commerce): Mr. Speaker, I intend to follow through on what I said on Friday. We are looking at this whole aspect. We have three or four isolated cases where we are, in a way, assisting the export of a commodity to a foreign country. In reply, that foreign company has indicated that it wants more of that product, but the multinational company's operation in Canada has had to tell us that it must direct those future sales to its parent company. As I said, we are taking steps to correct this
February 6, 1979

and I hope to have a further statement on that whole aspect later on.
.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, given the government's guidelines that it has had on the books for over four years now and which it has not enforced at all, I would like to ask the minister two things: First, will he name the companies involved which he referred to last Friday; and secondly, of equal importance considering that last year branch plants of foreign-owned firms in Canada shipped out more than $4 billion in royalties, management fees and interest payments, will the minister assure the House that the government intends to get specific commitments from such companies that they will, for example, perform a certain percentage of their research and development in Canada and export a certain percentage of their products from Canada where they are making the profits, instead of from the parent company whether it is in the United States or elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO CREATE JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want the hon. member or this House to believe that I think branch plants are a bad thing. That is not the case at all. In fact, there is not a community in Canada that would not allow the development of a branch plant in its area. I receive requests all the time from community leaders asking if some way or another I can direct a manufacturing plant into their community to assist growth and employment in their area.
What I did say was that there are some multinational corporations which must abide by the rules laid down by their parent company and which do not appear to be very conducive to Canada's export trade in the years ahead, and that we are taking steps to correct that aspect.
With regard to research and development, we would like to encourage its growth as much as possible in Canada, but we must have the end product of research and development, which is that it creates jobs. We must look at research and development in terms of creating jobs, and then the product of that research and development creating many more jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General and concerns the Boeing pay-offs.
The court of the District of Columbia in the United States, on July 25, 1978, ordered Boeing to file a deposition disclosing "any statistics of two consulting contracts with the same consultant providing for payments of compensation under each contract for the same services, designed to facilitate the payment of money into accounts maintained by the consultant outside his home country."
In reply to this, the Boeing company in a deposition to the SEC stated, inter alia, "The company executed two consulting agreements in connection with aircraft sales in Canada." In view of this, can the Solicitor General explain his remark of yesterday when he said, "I have no indication that any improper payments were made," or does he consider that getting paid
2920

a second time for one job and salting the money away in a foreign bank is a proper payment?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand by the statement I made yesterday. If the hon. gentleman has any allegation or proof of any allegation that could be investigated further by the RCMP, I invite him to bring it forward.
The investigation has been conducted properly by the RCMP. They have reviewed every lead made available to them. A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I should like to clear up a couple of points.
Is it the fact that the Solicitor General knows the individual who received the double payments, but is unable to frame a charge, or does the Solicitor General agree that an illegal act has been performed but he is unable to identify the crook?

subsubtopic: BOEING CONTRACT-EXPLANATION OF "IMPROPER PAYMENTS"

subsubtopic: MR. MAZANKOWSKI-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT-ALLEGED USE OF UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that yesterday I drew to your attention the choice of language which was used by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and I thought he might rise today to respond to the invitation extended both by yourself and by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen). Yesterday I did not have the benefit of reading the exchange which took place. 1 did, however, raise my point of order at that time on the basis of my best recollection. I drew attention to the fact that the minister had accused me of distorting the facts and of being irresponsible in interpreting a statement which he had made in the House on December 5, 1977. In examining yesterday's Hansard I find that the minister not only suggested distortion but also accused me of insisting on distortions. At page 2869 of Hansard the minister is recorded as having said the following:
Once again, the hon. member insists on distorting the situation terribly-
Later the minister said that 1 was "restating what is false", and he asked me to "stop stating these falsehoods". Yesterday Your Honour suggested that the matter should be held in abeyance, and Your Honour anticipated that perhaps the minister might respond today. He has not risen in his place, so I wish to raise the issue again on the basis of having examined yesterday's Hansard.
I see two issues in this matter. I see a responsibility on the part of the minister to put the facts of the matter into an accurate perspective. I attempted to do that yesterday. I put on the record the statement to which I had referred in my question, that statement being found at page 1534 of Hansard for December 5, 1977, which is the following:
I have instructed that additional inspectors be hired and a significant number of them made available to the north.

February 6, 1979
Point of Order-Mr. Mazankowski
Yesterday in response to the question I posed, the minister suggested or implied that his commitment to hire additional inspectors was in relation only to the northern part of Ontario. Fie suggested, therefore, that I was distorting facts and stating a falsehood.
However, on the basis of the information we have there has clearly been a reduction in the number of inspectors since that time, and the statement the minister made as recorded at page 1534 indicates distinctly and categorically that he had ordered the hiring of inspectors, some of whom would be assigned to the northern Ontario region but not specifically limited to the northern Ontario region. There is, therefore, a clear contradiction, and I think the minister should recognize that.
I think it is quite clear that the minister was imputing motives when he used these words:
Once again, the hon. member insists on distorting the situation terribly-
First, the minister has no proof of that. Second, in my view his remarks were clearly unparliamentary.
Citation 320(2) of the fifth edition of Beauchesne, which has just recently been issued, states at page 105:
Since 1958, it has been ruled unparliamentary to use the following expressions:
Then at page 106 we find under the heading "distort" the words "deliberate distortion" and "deliberately distorted". The word "false' is dealt with at page 107, and the words "false statement" are included. In my opinion the words "the hon. member insists on distorting the situation terribly" have the effect of implying the same meaning as "deliberate distortion". To ratify that assumption I refer Your Honour to the Concise Oxford Dictionary and the definition of the word "deliberate" which, in short form, is "intentional". The meaning of the word "insist", according to the Concise Oxford Dictionary , is "to maintain positively". In my view both expressions involve an intention. If "deliberate distortion" is unparliamentary, I believe it is unparliamentary because it imputes to an hon. member an intention to distort. To maintain positively is to intend to distort, and therefore in my view that language is just as offensive or just as unparliamentary as the word "deliberate".
I believe that in his somewhat usual intemperate outburst the minister was perhaps overcome by emotion and a little sensitive to the situation. However, as one who is very distinguished in the field of law as a law professor and as one who should certainly be setting an example by obeying the laws of the land and the rules of parliamentary tradition, I think the minister should do the honourable thing and withdraw his offensive words. Because there clearly was a deliberate attempt on his part to impute motives, and I was not doing that.
My question was phrased with the utmost sincerity. The matter of aviation safety in Canada is very important. It is rather unfair of the minister to suggest that it was an attack to deliberately destroy or malign statistics and interpretations which might or might not have been placed upon his statement. So I certainly suggest you consider it, sir, and if you find

that the words are unparliamentary-I believe they are-then I think the minister should do the honourable thing and withdraw his remarks.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: MR. MAZANKOWSKI-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT-ALLEGED USE OF UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has now switched from a discussion of a point of order along the lines he raised yesterday to raising some issue in relation to parliamentary and unparliamentary language. I do not know whether or not he gave notice of it to Your Honour, but he certainly did not to me. I have not reflected on the language and cannot deal with that matter at all, so I will simply content myself with dealing with the point of order which the hon. member raised yesterday.
Surely any fair minded member would realize that I was reacting strongly to a suggestion by the hon. member that I had been in breach of a commitment. I did react strongly because I knew that that could not be true. I did not have the words and the passages before me to which the hon. member had referred because he did not give notice of the fact that he was going to refer to them; but the hon. member had those passages before him, and in particular, as he noted yesterday, he relied on words of mine quoted in Hansard at page 1534 where I am reported to have stated:
I have instructed that additional inspectors be hired and a significant number of them made available to the north.
If the hon. member has asked me whether I had done as I had committed myself to do, namely, instruct that additional inspectors be hired and a significant number of them be made available to the north, he would have received a firm, positive answer that I did so. He did not ask that question, perhaps because he knew that the answer was indeed positive. But clearly he has no evidence whatsoever-

subsubtopic: MR. MAZANKOWSKI-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT-ALLEGED USE OF UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE
speechtext: You are imputing motives.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: MR. MAZANKOWSKI-STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF TRANSPORT-ALLEGED USE OF UNPARLIAMENTARY LANGUAGE
speechtext:

I say that when using those words, he twisted them to mean that I was in breach of a commitment which he alleges I made in relation to the number of inspectors. He was being unfair. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would argue on a point of order that this report of the standing committee is out of order, and that therefore the motion to concur in it cannot be debated. First, I would refer you to Beauchesne, citation 323(1), which reads as follows:
A committee report may be ruled out of order though it has been received by the House, and the motion to concur therein cannot be entertained.
Now the thrust of this particular quotation is quite clear- that the simple fact that a committee report has been accepted in this place does not mean of itself that the report is in fact in order, i will argue that the motion moved by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) for concurrence in the report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs is out of order.
First of all, I should like to quote Beauchesne's citation 304, subsections (1), (2) and (4), to prove my point. Citation 304(1) reads as follows:
A committee can only consider those matters which have been committed to it by the House.
Quite evidently Bill C-204 does not include any reference whatsoever to the matter referred to the committee in the motion, that is, the penitentiary system dealing with children and adults. The bill does not even touch that particular matter, and therefore the committee has given consideration in preparing this motion to a subject that has not been referred to it, and it is not entitled to do so.
Citation 304(2) reads:
A committee is bound by, and is not at liberty to depart from, the order of reference. In the case of a select committee upon a bill, the bill committed to it is itself the order of reference to the committee, who must report it with or without amendment to the House.
2928

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report
Under this subsection of Beauchesne, quite clearly the report before us is neither an amendment nor a report of the bill referred to the committee. It is quite evident the report is neither an amendment to Bill C-204 nor a report respecting Bill C-204. For those reasons, it goes beyond the terms of reference of the particular committee.
I should like to refer to citation 304(4) of Beauchesne's fourth edition which reads as follows:
Sometimes a committee may have to obtain leave from the House to make a special report when its order of reference is limited in scope.
This is a very operative section of Beauchesne because it makes very clear that under circumstances such as we face today in the House, if a committee wishes to expand its terms of reference or go beyond the terms it already has in making a report or in any other activity, then it must seek leave of the House to do so. Therefore, it is quite clear unanimous consent would be required before the motion of concurrence can be put to the House. I suggest this motion cannot be put without such concurrence.
Further, the committee has gone beyond its terms of reference by using the words of the motion itself, which seems to be quite evident when it considered the advisability of amplifying and enlarging its said reference. This seems to be a very open and tacit admission that in fact an attempt is being made by the motion to go beyond and enlarge the committee's terms of reference, which attempt is prohibited under the rules of the House. In passing the second report, the committee is admitting openly that it is attempting to go beyond the terms of reference given it by the House.
In my judgment, this motion is one without clear direction and meaning. I find it very strange that the second report requests the House to consider the advisability of amplifying and enlarging its said reference. That seems to be very strange wording. If in fact the motion were put, and if concurrence with the report were accepted by the House, it would not really do anything. It would not do anything because the motion would not enlarge the terms of reference of the committee. The motion is not directed toward the committee; it is directed toward the House's considering the advisability of such a matter. I do not know the mechanism the House would have before it to consider the advisability. Even on that practical ground, I would say that the motion of concurrence would have no meaning in terms of achieving an expansion of the terms of reference of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
This motion for concurrence cannot be put at this time under the rules of the House, under the precedents I have cited, and therefore the motion cannot be debated.

speechtext:
Order, please. I do not know if it is necessary to go into a lengthy discussion on this point of order, but we can set aside one part of the argument immediately. I understand the point that a committee seized of a bill in the ordinary motion of reference of a bill to a committee is under somewhat strict terms of reference respecting that. It cannot
(Mr. Caftk.j
attempt to launch into other investigations, or probably it cannot even come back to the House. I am not trying to make law, but the precedent cited respecting that is very clear.
In the ordinary course of second reading, when a bill is referred to a committee for clause by clause study, the committee has certain limitations under which it must act and must report the bill back with or without amendment. To begin with, I understand that this is not a situation in which a bill has been referred to a committee, but the subject matter of the bill has been referred. That is an important distinction to start with, because obviously the committee is not under that stricture. That being the case, it is a committee to which a subject has been referred.
When a subject is referred to a committee, and when the committee looking at the subject indicates that it feels constrained by the first term of reference, which is the reference of the subject matter, and that it wants to acknowledge to the House that its terms of reference are restricted, that it is seeking additional powers, and that it ought not to attempt to exercise those powers without the permission of the House, then the committee reports to the House asking the House to give or consider giving those extended powers.
I would have to be persuaded that a committee cannot do so. That would be very difficult to do. A committee seized of a subject matter, which seeks to extend its term of reference and wants additional authority, must come back to the House. Having done so, it reports to the House and indicates; "This is what we have examined, and we find our hands are slightly tied and we need additional power".
For example, I am sure there have been numerous occasions in the past when an order of reference has been given to a committee to examine and inquire into a certain subject matter in Ottawa, and the committee finds that it wants to travel. Properly it comes back to the House and indicates that it would like authority to travel and to hold meetings in various areas of the country; can it do so? Obviously it must be beyond the original terms of reference or the committee would not be coming back to the House for further permission. It cannot do it without coming back to the House, and if it cannot come back to the House to ask, then I do not know what the committee can do or what course it can follow.
This report of the committee does not tie the hands of the House, but I do not think that is the concern of the Chair. In the end the report recommends or asks the House to consider the advisability of extending the committee's terms of reference. Therefore, concurrence in the report would put the House in the position of having to consider the advisability of extending the terms of reference. It does not constitute a motion for an extended term of reference. I accept that point, as I think the House does. But that is not a procedural matter; that is the content of the report. The report is that the committee seeks an extended term of reference.
If the committee were seeking an extended term of reference which might be argued was not in any way relevant to the subject matter, we might be on different ground; but we are not. Obviously if the committee wanted to inquire into some-
February 6, 1979

thing which was entirely without relevance, it might be argued on a matter of relevance that there might be some difficulty.
Basically I must find in the circumstances that this is not a situation in which a bill has been referred to a committee, but rather one in which a subject matter has been referred. It is a situation in which the committee acknowledges it needs or wants an additional term of reference. Also the committee acknowledges that in order to get it, it must first come to the House. That is what the committee is doing by way of this report. I do not see how a committee can be expected to act otherwise. I do not think I could make any ruling which would prevent a committee from doing so, provided that it is relevant.
Finally, I accept the point that concurrence in this report does nothing more than leave the House in the position of considering the advisability of extending the terms of reference. In my opinion, it would not constitute a direction that that order of reference must be taken as having been extended without some additional motion. That would be the disposition I would make.
I do not think we ought to spend a lot of time attempting to enter arguments into that position. 1 accept the last point that the content of the report is not a directive to the House. Since this is a situation in which a subject matter was referred to a committee, and since the committee acknowledges by this report that it must come to the House for expanded terms of reference, procedurally it is a proper course to follow and the motion should be put.

I cannot resist the temptation to say that any time the government has a weak case it puts up the deputy government House leader to make its statement. I am surprised he has not caught on by now, Mr. Speaker, but perhaps he will after today.
What we have before the House, Mr. Speaker, is a motion for concurrence in the second report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. This is necessary for the purpose of conforming with parliamentary procedure. If you scratch away the parliamentary niceties and brush off all the parliamentary foss and look underneath, what you will find is a mini-revolt by one of the standing committees of this House.
What the members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, under the distinguished and learned chairmanship of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), is saying, in the words of Howard Beale, is: "We are mad as hell, we are not going to take it any more, we are fed up with being ignored by the government."
Why is the committee acting this way? Why is that standing committee, made up of such distinguished jurists as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), and the hon. member for Toron-to-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), not to mention the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn), acting in this way? We even have a "sea lawyer" on that committee from Newfoundland, Mr. Speaker, who perhaps deserves some mention in his own right. Why are those members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs interrupting their proceedings under the terms of reference regarding the subject matter of Bill C-204 to report back to the House? As I suggest, ostensibly it is to broaden the terms of reference to include the matter of the incarceration of children and the penal system as it relates to both children and adults.
Why did we feel that was necessary? We felt it necessary because we are involved in a most interesting and meaningful study. The committee is involved, during the first months of the International Year of the Child, in studying the whole question of children's rights and how we as a developed and enlightened nation treat our children.
The question came up during the course of the proceedings on the subject matter of Bill C-204, which I had the honour to sponsor, as to what became of the last order of reference before the committee. What happened to the committee's very learned and comprehensive report on the penitentiary system

in Canada? More particularly, what happened to the recommendations contained in the report of the subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on the penitentiary system in Canada?
I was not a member of that subcommittee but my colleagues were, and they worked long and hard in the bipartisan way that has become characteristic of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs under its distinguished chairman. They worked long and hard in the pursuit of this order of reference that they received from the Elouse on October 21, 1976.
That committee travelled across the country and visited all of the major institutions in the Atlantic provinces, in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia. We who are charged by this House with pursuing the order of reference now before the standing committee and the subject matter of Bill C-204 have the right, indeed the obligation, to ask the government why it did not act upon the recommendations of the subcommittee regarding the penitentiary system in Canada. I intend to document this case because we do not want to diminish or take away in any manner the importance of the order of reference now before the committee, the subject matter of Bill C-204, an act respecting a bill of rights for children, but before we proceed to draft our recommendations in this connection we would like to know what the government intends to do with our order of reference. We have heard distinguished witnesses from across the country, we will be hearing from the Human Rights Commission and, if we are lucky, we may even hear from one of the ministers of the government. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) may decide to honour us with his presence although that has not been the case up to now. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), who has a special responsibility in this regard, may even honour us with her presence and tell us what the government proposes to do in the International Year of the Child and address some of the grave injustices which have crept into our system with respect to how we treat our children in this so-called enlightened society.
The fact of the matter is, sir, that we have a right and an obligation before we proceed any further to say, "Hold on, just a minute; before we play this government's game let's go back to the House and ask the government why they have not acted upon our last order of reference, our last recommendations contained in the standing report of the subcommittee into the penitentiary system of Canada.
I have been an active member of committees of this House since 1 was resurrected in 1968. 1 objected to the new rules of the House, which at the time were imposed by closure, because by taking out of the House the right to membership in committees we were destroying the very collegiality that was the core of the committee system whereby the committees built up this collegiality and expertise by the tenure of the membership. The subject matter of one of the private members' bill dealt with pornography and obscenity under the Criminal Code. We heard witnesses. We travelled to Toronto and we saw evidence first-hand. We realized the gravity of the situation, and we made recommendations to the House.
To date those recommendations have not been acted upon. Why? Surely, we have a right to know why the government has not brought in the necessary amendments to the Criminal Code in pursuance of the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs as a result of the subject matter of the private member's bill dealing with the whole question of pornography and obscenity.

The recommendations of that order of reference were again as a result of a private member's initiative. I can document all of the recommendations of that committee which dealt with child abuse. It is a very serious matter and one that we have been seized with in our deliberations of the subject matter of Bill C-204.
Why has the government not acted upon those recommendations? The House thought that it was important enough to refer the matter to the justice committee, and the justice committee thought that is was important enough to hear witnesses and was seized with the urgency of the matter. They thought that it was important enough to bring in meaningful recommendations to the House which the House concurred in and which the government promptly proceeded to ignore. Why? We have the right to ask why the government continues to ignore the recommendations of the standing committees of this House.
I have another set of recommendations, which, if I may modestly say, are a result of my own initiative. They are with respect to a private member's bill which I brought before this House. The House, after a number of debates at second reading stage, agreed to have the subject matter of the bill referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. That is the bill-I am glad to see that the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve) is in her seat- relating to amendments to the Broadcasting Act dealing with advertising directed at children. The House and the govern-

ment thought that it was important enough to refer it to the committee. The committee thought that it was important enough to examine witnesses from all over the country. Indeed, from many different parts of the world experts were brought in and we heard evidence from them. We saw evidence with our own eyes.
As a result of bringing together all this evidence, we as a committee came to the conclusion that advertising directed at children on television was immoral and had no place in an enlightened society such as Canada's. We recommended that it be banned, and our recommendations were concurred in by the House on July 12, 1973 by a unanimous motion. We recommend that the CRTC pass regulations which provide that advertising not be directed exclusively at children. We made other recommendations which I will not take the time to describe, but they are there for all to see.
What has the government done by way of acting on these recommendations which were not only unanimously passed by a committee after exhaustive studies and many witnesses, but unanimously concurred in by the House? Why does the Minister of Communications not stand up in her place in the House, in this the International Year of the Child, and tell us why the government has not implemented the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs passed by the House in July, 1973 requesting that advertising directed at children be eliminated? That was six years ago.
It is interesting and worth noting that only last year the federal communications commission and the federal trade commission in the United States came to the very conclusion that we as a parliamentary committee came to in 1973, that this kind of advertising should be banned. Yet we still have the shame and the scandal of our children being used by the broadcasting industry, the cereal manufacturers, the toy manufacturers and other advertisers as surrogates. Perhaps the minister will tell us before this debate is over why the government in this the International Year of the Child has not acted upon the recommendation of a standing committee of this House which were unanimously adopted by this House which would end this form of exploitation of children.

Surely the members of standing committees of this House have a right to know, before we proceed with any further studies and before we proceed with any further recommendations, why the government ignores these recommendations.
That is why this second report of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs is before the House at this time. That is why the committee unanimously, in a bipartisan way, interrupted its proceedings in pursuit of its order of reference on the subject matter of Bill C-204, to get this report before the House so that we could hold the Solicitor General accountable for his failure to act on recommendations with respect to penitentiaries; so that we could hold the Minister of Communications accountable for not acting on recommendations of the broadcasting committee with respect to advertising directed at children.
The members of this House are mad, Mr. Speaker. The hon. lady opposite, for whom I have great respect, cautions me to keep it non-partisan. I am dealing with the government. Our joint grievance is against the government. That, I suppose, by its very nature will make it partisan because I am opposed to the government. I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt), who was one of the outstanding members of that committee and was most diligent in participating in the penitentiary study, and who has been a good deputy chairman of the committee, is one of the members who will be contributing to the debate today. I am sure she will have her own grievance as to why the subject of the committee report has been ignored.
Surely the whole broad range of this debate has to do with the relevance of parliament itself. I think it can and must be said that, as a result of the rules changes imposed by closure in 1968, parliamentary committees were supposed to assume a

new importance. In their legislative capacity they have functioned well in terms of dealing with government legislation. They are very restricted in that particular case, as was enunciated by Your Honour in the ruling on the point of order. But with respect to what should be their equally important function of dealing with the estimates, they have been a dismal failure. We have not influenced or changed one single estimate of this government because the rules do not permit us to do so. Under the rules of the House all estimates are deemed to have been passed and reported back to the House by committees as of midnight on May 31.
What a farce that is, Mr. Speaker. Is it any wonder that government members and opposition members alike are fed up and do not want to be a part of this meaningless charade? That is all it is, Mr. Speaker, a meaningless charade.
I believe that parliamentary committees under our system should have an ongoing investigatory function. Their terms of reference should be laid on the floor of the House at the commencement of each session so that annual reports would be automatically referred to them. There should be an expenditures committee to work in concert with the Standing Committee on Public Accounts in order to examine expenditures on an ongoing basis.
That raises the whole question of the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization. Where is it? Why has it not been called? Why has the government not brought in a reference to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization? Only the government can bring in such a reference; only the government can manage the business of the House. The committee has not met this session and did not have a chance to report in the last session, notwithstanding the fact that it put together a very meaningful set of recommendations which would change the whole procedure of this House and bring it more in keeping with the live televising of debates which is affecting this place so profoundly.
What we are debating here today is this government's attitude to-one could almost say contempt for-parliament. Certainly, I have tried to demonstrate its contempt for parliamentary committees; it can only be described as contemptuous. How else can we explain the fact that the reference before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs dealing with a bill of rights for children in this the International Year of the Child has not heard from the Minister of National Health and Welfare who has responsibility in this area, or from the Minister of Justice who has responsibility for the laws of this country? That speaks to their whole attitude toward the committees of this House.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say first of all that I am very glad to take part in this debate and to speak after the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I want to say immediately to the hon. gentleman that I fully intend to support the motion under review, and that contrary to what he suggested in his remarks, we have already implemented most of the recommendations of the parliamentary subcommittee he mentioned.
The reasons I support this motion are twofold: First, because this motion before us says a great deal about the importance and urgency attached to the subcommittee report by members of the standing committee, and I share that sense of importance and urgency; second, because 1 am most concerned with the inaccurate impression left by some of the media, and regretfully by some members of this House, that nothing is being done to implement reforms in the penitentiary system, and that the report of the subcommittee is being ignored by the government.
Let me elaborate briefly on both points. Hon. members will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the report of the subcommittee resulted from a motion made in this House by my predecessor more than two years ago. The subcommittee report was tabled in the House in June, 1977 and each of its 65 recommendations was responded to in an initial way in August of that year. There have been a number of documents tabled before the
Concurrence in Committee Report Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs relating to the implementation of the recommendations. The latest is the one I circulated at the beginning of this week dated January, 1979 and which I believe each member of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs has received.
In his initial response my predecessor made known his acceptance in whole or in part of 53 recommendations. He made it very clear that the officers and staff of the Canadian penitentiary service and all others concerned in the ministry of the Solicitor General will spare no effort in the implementation of the recommendations.
In November and December, 1977, the standing committee examined supplementary estimates and on that occasion held several meetings to consider a detailed recommendation-byrecommendation progress report on the implementation. That report was tabled by my predecessor. Just eight days after assuming office, less than one year ago, I attended before the committee. At that time I stated:
I strongly endorse the statement of support made by my predecessor with respect to the general thrust and philosophy of the report, and I share his sense of urgent commitment to far reaching reform in corrections.
Since last February I have tabled two further recommendation-by-recommendation progress reports: last March at the time of the main estimates, and last November at the time of the supplementary estimates. Further reports are being prepared in readiness for the standing committee's consideration of further supplementary estimates and main estimates for the fiscal year 1979-80. Therefore, I will be appearing before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on the supplementary estimates, which will be tabled shortly, and also on the main estimates. At that time undoubtedly the committee will be examining the progress made in the implementation of the subcommittee's report.
But let us not look at the words contained in those reports; instead let us look at the actions. In spite of the difficulty of introducing major change into a complex system involving over 10,000 employees, more than 9,400 inmates and over 7,000 persons released under supervision, a large number of important changes have already been implemented in the Canadian corrections system since publication of the report. Some of these actions culminated in months or years of preparatory work already under way and given impetus by the report; others responded to specific recommendations contained in the report.
In this regard I will explain more fully. Independent chairmen have been appointed in all maximum security institutions to hear serious and flagrant disciplinary cases. A pilot grievance procedure introduced at the Prince Albert penitentiary in Saskatchewan has proven successful and will be implemented throughout the system this year. Incidentally, that is an undertaking 1 have given to the committee. An inspector general was appointed last spring. He has now conducted more than ten studies at the behest of the commissioner of the penitentiary. Inmate committees, citizen advisory committees and segregation review boards have been established at almost all institutions.

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report
A major reorganization of national and regional headquarters has taken place, placing the institution under the direct command of a regional director general who in turn is directly responsible to the commissioner. Major new impetus has been given to the industries program to make it more productive, more efficient and more meaningful. Vocational training programs have been re-examined to tie in with the industries program and to get valid accreditation from relevant provincial jurisdiction. Just last week 1 attended in Vancouver in order to announce the closing of the Kingston prison for women, which again is in accordance with the recommendations of the subcommittee.
The probation period for new employees was extended from six months to 24 months. A new code of conduct for employees has been developed. That code has been fully discussed with members within the institutions. Five days per year of refresher training for employees has been instituted. This was done notwithstanding the fact that they have had a shortage of man-years of a result of government cutbacks and expenditures. We have had to find individual posts for training positions to accommodate that recommendation, and that was no mean effort on the part of the Canadian correctional staff.
Emergency response teams have been set up in all regions and most institutions. The "no deals" policy on hostage taking has been implemented. A wholly revised construction program was developed saving the taxpayer more than $200 million in capital costs and $60 million per year in operating costs.
New procedural safeguards for parole hearings were instituted in regulations under the Parole Act. Appointments were made of community representatives to parole panels in cases involving dangerous inmates. Treaties were signed for the exchange of offenders with the United States and Mexico in accordance with the Transfer of Offenders Act. Expansion of alternatives to incarceration available in the Criminal Code are contained in Bill C-21 now before the Elouse.

And I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that the process to implement the recommendations of Bill C-21 could be speeded up so that we would really profit by the clauses concerning community service orders contained in the bill.

I could go on, Mr. Speaker, to outline other specific actions which have been instituted and implemented already in response to the report of the subcommittee, but I hope that I have made my point. A great deal has already been accomplished. I could also go on to outline other actions that are near to being implemented, but perhaps that kind of enumeration should await the meetings to be held by the standing committee as a result of passage of this motion, if it is so passed.

speechtext:
I find this a highly interesting question because the hon. member for St. John's East said that he had a responsibility, as member of the opposition, to oppose, and that regarding this report he had to take a stance. At least that is how I understood it, that he had to take a stance as an adversary, as a legitimate member of the opposition, and I recognize that. But as the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mrs. Holt) indicated, there is a tendency among committee members not to take a partisan view but rather to try to improve the penitentiary system in collaboration with all members of parliament.
I certainly think that this should continue, but when I list all the advantages and all the basic changes we have introduced in the penitentiary system, I really question the intentions of opposition members who sit on that committee, because I am entirely committed, along with my officials, to implement changes according to the subcommittee's recommendations. I am fully committed to that and that has been one of my major concerns this past year. But when I see the lack of understanding shown by some opposition members in my own good faith and that of officials of the Canadian correctional service, I wonder if opposition members are really interested in ridding themselves of their partisanship and undertake the reforms suggested in their report.
Now for the second reason 1 support the motion. Because I had dedicated a great deal of effort over the past 12 months to implementation of the theme of the subcommittee report, and because I have seen at first hand the amount of effort put into its implementation by members of the Canadian correctional service it is with some degree of disappointment and frustration that I listen to suggestions that the government is doing nothing to further the goals set out by the parliamentary subcommittee. To my mind the frustration has been mutual because, undoubtedly, there has been frustration on the part of the committee. I have already recounted the support lent to the main theme and principles of the subcommittee report both by myself and by my predecessor. The main theme of the report, that of establishing and maintaining both a pervading attitude and a reality of professional discipline in corrections, is woven throughout the report's 200 pages, just as it unites the large number of specific initiatives taken by the government in response to the report. As I mentioned a few moments ago, we have already introduced several measures aimed at the creation of a highly disciplined, professional, career-oriented corrections service of the kind envisaged by the subcommittee.
I would be less than frank, however, if I failed to mention that in taking our responsibilities under the Penitentiary Act,

February 6, 1979

and in consequence of the system of responsible government under which we operate, it became clear to my predecessor and myself that some of the specific means suggested by the subcommittee were not the most appropriate or the most effective toward reaching the ends upon which we were all agreed. Because of this, I believe the altogether mistaken impression has been formed in some quarters that reform is not proceeding.
Perhaps I could give two examples. On December 10, 1978 I announced that the five-year construction program upon which the corrections service had embarked was undergoing major revision. In line with that revision a drastic cutback was made in the number of new institutions being planned, saving the taxpayer more than $225 million in capital costs and more than $60 million a year in operating costs. As part of the revision a decision was made to increase the maximum size of new institutions to 350 to 450 inmates, instead of the 250 inmates contemplated in the earlier program.
As I have pointed out, this decision as to capacity contrasted with earlier government policy and with the specific recommendation of the subcommittee, which supported the position taken earlier by the government. However, the earlier decision had not been supported by solid evidence that the smaller institutions were more effective in attaining correctional goals. In fact, the CCS undertook studies which revealed that no such evidence existed.
It is my view that a number of factors affect the success, or lack of success, of correctional institutions but that size is not the most important of these factors. Maybe it is not a very important factor at all, especially when we are talking not of a choice between small institutions and the huge 2,000 plus institutions which many American states operate, but rather of a choice between institutions of 250 inmates and institutions which have the capability of being expanded, should the demand warrant it, to a maximum of 450 inmates. I have made it clear that program quality would not be allowed to suffer, and I have also stressed the point that the living unit concept, another of the CCS policies supported by the subcommittee, would be used in all the new institutions. That is something on which I have insisted. In all the new buildings, even those designated as maximum security, the living unit concept is to be introduced.
I am sorry to say that some have interpreted this decision as a rejection of the fundamental philosophy contained in the subcommittee report. Most assuredly it is not. And this will not be the effect. It is because I am eager to clear up this confusion and correct this interpretation that I support the motion before us. I shall be willing to address this question fully when I appear again before the committee.
There have been suggestions that I have been interested in cutting back offender programs. To the contrary, hon. members will see from the close questioning of myself and my officials that I have been adamant in proceeding with the development of offender programs.
Let me give a second example. The subcommittee made several recommendations dealing with the organization and
Concurrence in Committee Report
management of the correctional service, and of these recommendations 24 and 26 formed the core. The main import of this second recommendation was to remove the corrections service from the public service so as to give it the kind of independence, identity and flexibility which the subcommittee saw as being essential to its reform.
Both my predecessor and myself felt some initial misgivings about that package of recommendations, not because we did not approve the goal being sought-we did share that goal and we said so very clearly-but because we were not convinced that the means suggested by the subcommittee were the best for achieving it. My predecessor established a senior interdepartmental working group to examine that package of recommendations. I have received its report and, after studying the issue myself, I have concluded that a different set of measures would better enable us to establish the kind of highly disciplined, more independent professional career service which is the ultimate objective.
On this question, I frankly admit a fundamental difference in opinion with the subcommittee. The subcommittee recommended that the CCS be removed from the jurisdiction of the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the Public Service Employment Act and set up on the model of the RCMP. However, it was silent on the question of the acquired union rights of CCS employees.
I would argue that the subcommittee did not adequately think through the implications of this crucial distinction between the CCS and the RCMP. We must bear in mind that only one third of the CCS staff are guards. The CCS has been unionized for more than a decade; the RCMP, never. If the recommendation of the subcommittee were implemented literally, the CCS would automatically come under the jurisdiction of part IV of the Canada Labour Code which gives the employer rather less control in certain areas than do the Public Service Staff Relations Act and the Public Service Employment Act.
In the alternative, CCS employees would have to be stripped of many rights acquired and exercised for more than a decade. This drastic step was never advocated by the subcommittee, and with reason, because advocating such a step would mean that it would be impossible to manage the Canadian correctional service. There would be a very negative reaction within the service which would detrimentally affect morale within that service and the whole operation of the Canadian correctional service.
In light of this I suggested to the standing committee as long ago as last March that a number of very significant steps can be taken within the current framework of employer-employee relations to bring about the result both the committee and I are eager to achieve.
The steps are as follows: Establish in legislation a new and distinct corrections "family" category for all employees providing for the care, custody and training of offenders; establish the CCS as a separate employer under the law, thus giving the

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report
CCS direct responsibility and accountability for collective bargaining and staff relations; including the new code of professional conduct in regulations under the Penitentiary Act; fully delegate staffing authority for the new employee category to the CCS from the Public Service Commission, thus enabling the CCS to recruit more directly and more in accordance with its own needs and priorities.
Implementation of this package of changes will further the development of the disciplined professional career service the subcommittee was aiming for. It is a very complex and large task to introduce such major changes into a large scale, highly decentralized and very complex organization with, to say the least, a difficult operating mandate to pursue, but this work is proceeding apace, as I will be glad to demonstrate to the standing committee.
The point of all this is that the quite erroneous interpretation has been placed on these developments that the subcommittee report is being rejected or, perhaps worse, ignored by the government because these differences over specific means have appeared. This impression is one I very much regret, and it is also one I wholly reject.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, obviously there is a misunderstanding here because the reservations I expressed at the first meeting of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs on two of the basic recommendations have been given a false interpretation. These reservations have been interpreted as a complete rejection of the entire report. That is not at all the case. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, even as far as recommendations numbers 24 and 26 are concerned, I fully support the principle underlying them and, if I may say so, I am fully geared to implementing them. Mr. Speaker, I would like the House to realize all the efforts that not only I but all my officers are making to implement those recommendations.

Furthermore, I think it is a most dangerous impression, as the subcommittee itself pointed out, because a great deal of the success or failure of reform depends heavily on attitudes.
I have tried today to stress the fact that penitentiary reform is the most important of the responsibilities I have as minister responsible for the CCS. I have also gone to some length to give my view of the basis for what I see as a major and regrettable misinterpretation of some of the actions of the government and of the government's intentions in this regard.

I shall not go any further today, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want to create controversy. I would like to persuade my colleagues on both sides of the House that I intend to implement the recommendations of the committee, that despite the allegations made by the hon. member for St. John's East. I do recognize that the rules of the House make it possible to undertake a thorough study of the recommendations to further implement these recommendations. We are prepared to appear before the committee at its request in order to justify our

course of action, our implementing these recommendations. I simply urge hon. members on this side as well as on the other side to recognize that we operate within a huge, very complex system and that such fundamental changes as those put forward by the subcommittee are indeed very difficult to achieve. I further urge hon. members to recognize that these changes require a great deal of attention, of patience, of tolerance, of understanding from all the involved and interested parties.

Mr. Speaker, I will not deal with the question of relevance.
