February 6, 1979

On the matter of how much of this report has been adopted and how much has not, I think it is important to remember that there are 65 recommendations of varying value. Some of those recommendations are very minor; they are easy to accomplish. Some of them recommend very serious changes, and the committee knew that that would be more difficult and would take a longer period of time. However, 1 submit that on any fair evaluation of the reaction to this unanimous report only tinkering recommendations have been adopted, and I think this committee will find, when it goes back inside the penitentiary system, that there has not been any change at all. In fact, I would go further and say that we in this country are in danger of being in the kind of situation we were in when the subcommittee commenced its investigation in 1977. I worry about the reports which are emanating from the maximum security systems. I worry about the potential for another crisis in the system.
One of the difficulties in trying to determine what the government's reaction to the report has been is, as I say, the value of the various recommendations. This was a bipartisan committee. It was a non-partisan committee, with more than two parties represented. I am sure that was a slip of the tongue on the part of my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). It is vital that we look at the initial unanimous reaction of the committee to the study, and that was that a crisis exists within the Canadian penitentiary system. It was on the word "crisis" that the government demurred; the government said they cannot agree there is a crisis in the system.
From that point on the reaction of the committee members was one of disappointment, because we had looked at it on the ground and we felt that perhaps the government should have accepted the reaction of the committee members who had spent such a long time on the study. We had visited 17 institutions and interviewed 2,000 witnesses; it was a very extensive study.
It is interesting also to remember that none of the members of that committee got everything they wanted in that report. Compromises were made by all members of the committee, but we felt that in the interests of the country we should bury our differences which we have in the House from time to time, and we found the things on which we could agree for the good of the system and the good of the country. That is why we have been concerned about the fact that the Solicitor General does not have the same kind of reaction, the same kind of concern, that we have in looking at it on the ground.
The Solicitor General indicated in his remarks that he had just been out west where he had announced the phasing out of the women's prison, but I do not recall whether he had had a visit with the guards of, for example, the British Columbia penitentiary while he was there putting out his press release and having interviews on radio and television. I am not sure whether he did a tour of the B.C. pen, but if he did not he should have because one must be inside those institutions to
Concurrence in Committee Report know what is going on. There is no value in relying on rumour and all the things that emanate from there; you have to be on the ground.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order with reference to the remarks of the hon. gentleman. May I say that I have been to the B.C. pen and I also took the opportunity when I was in Vancouver to announce that I fully intend to close the B.C. pen in order to alleviate the concerns of the hon. gentleman.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My apologies to the minister, Mr. Speaker. 1 was not aware he had actually toured the B.C. pen and I give him credit for having done so. However, I think he should also have met with the correctional officers in that institution because they have some serious grievances they want to take up with the Solicitor General.
In any event, let us examine which recommendations have been adopted and which have not. Let us take a look at the record. On August 5, 1977, the then solicitor general said: "I have accepted 53 of the recommendations in whole or in part." In February of 1978, the present Solicitor General said: "Thirty-seven of the recommendations have been implemented or are in the process of being implemented." Now we are down to 37. Again, in October of 1978 the Solicitor General said: "As of the end of October, 1978, 22 recommendations have been completely implemented."
Let us examine what really happened. Of those 22 recommendations implemented by the end of October, 1978, two were implemented as pilot projects, one was rejected but called implemented and at least three implementations are questionable: The staff and inmates identification tags, the no deal rule on hostage taking, the completion of post-analysis and dual responsibility for programs and security matters for all staff. This leaves a total of 14 recommendations implemented of the 65 over a period of a year and eight months since the subcommittee reported to the House.
I am sure the Solicitor General and I can get into a rather lengthy debate about the quality of implementation and about what implementation really means. I accept that as probably the kind of argument anyone can have, but the reality is that a careful analysis of the report still leaves only 14 recommendations implemented and the major recommendations have not really been touched.
Let me give some examples. When we recommended early retirement for those who work within the institutions, we asked: Why should the RCMP have a special advantage in terms of their pension when someone who works inside those institutions, who faces hostility every day and who has one of the toughest jobs in the country has to serve until he is 60 years old? We found a great many people within the institutions who deserve to have a chance at a second career or at early retirement. That was absolutely key to doing something about the morale within the institutions. We were seriously concerned about the horribly low morale in the penitentiary system. Where has the recommendations with regard to early retirement gone? That is a fundamental question. If you are

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report changing some of the conditions of the people who work within the institutions, you cannot pick and choose; you cannot take the pieces you like and reject those which, for some reason or other, you do not like. I submit that that has been the attitude of the government.
Let me give another example. The Solicitor General in the course of his remarks mentioned that the department has gone to a regional director system. Allegedly, that was some kind of an acceptance of our report. In fact, it flies in the face of our report; it goes in exactly the opposite direction. We recommended that regions be de-emphasized. We recommended that the director of a penitentiary be master of his own institution. He is on the line, he takes the risks, he must make those important decisions. Instead of regions being phased out, the opposite has happened. There has been an increase of about 20 per cent since our report came out. Not only has there not been acceptance of our recommendations, but decisions have been taken going in the opposite direction. That was why members of our committee have been seriously frustrated by the reaction of the government.
Now I want to deal with a couple of the other recommendations. One of them may be typical of a great deal of what is happening in the Solicitor General's department. It sounds like a minor thing. We recommended that inmates and guards should wear tags to identify themselves in the event of some problem arising, such as a scuffle, an assault, etc. What was the response? We were told that this has been accepted 100 per cent and an order went out that everyone wear name tags. First of all, the guards did not want to wear them, then the prisoners did not want to wear them, so they decided they would make the guards wear them but not the prisoners. In fact, I have recently received a letter from the Solicitor General stating the following:
Because of these problems, and after extended discussions, it was decided that staff will wear the plastic name tags as part of their uniform, and that inmates will not be required actually to wear name tags but, instead, must have their identification card in their possession at all times and produce it on demand.
Again it is a simple question of morale: Why should one side be required to wear the tags and not the other side? That is how you destroy morale within an institution. That is one of those famous recommendations which we were told has been adopted. A typical kind of reaction was, "We love your report; we are adopting your recommendation". In fact that was not the case. The people have been misled and the country is being misled because of the inadequate response to the report.
I mentioned earlier the concerns about the present condition of the institutions. I will read a letter that came into my hands, and I will not identify the people in it because, as we all know, of the sensitivity within the institution. This letter refers to the present condition of the Millhaven institution. As an ex-committee member I quote from the letter as follows:
I know and feel the mood of the joint. It's ready to blow and harder than ever before. I don't believe anything can stop it. I am just letting you know in advance. It could make interesting news. Merry Christmas.

That is typical not of one institution but of four or five maximum security institutions in Canada. Not one serious incident occurred while the committee investigated the institutions of Canada. They were cool, they knew someone cared and was paying attention. They knew that some action was happening regarding these problems. We as members of parliament, the Solicitor General and his department, must go back and convince everyone inside those institutions that we care and will change the situation.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It cannot be done with three-quarters of an hour of rhetoric in the House. It cannot be done by indicating that it has been adopted, everything is fine, and by throwing around the soft soap. One cannot do that because the penitentiaries are too dangerous. One cannot "con a con". One cannot con people inside those institutions because they live in those conditions and know which changes have taken place. It is important to have another reference. I am not suggesting a long one. It could be a short one. But it is important because again we will be provided with an opportunity to look inside and see whether conditions have changed, whether we can do anything to effect some change in the atmosphere. I do not mean to be overdramatic, but perhaps we can save someone's life. One must remember that many lives have been lost within the Canadian penitentiary service.
I should like to refer to the prison expansion program to which the Solicitor General referred. The government recently cut back the program, but we still are looking at $302.7 million. I do not agree with the philosophy that we should go to larger institutions, because that will not be the absolute key. It is what goes on within the walls which is the important key. I do not believe we should spend another dollar constructing any more prisons in the country until we do something about changing the conditions inside the existing ones.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I agree we need more prisons and that the dungeon prisons need to be phased out at some time, but we cannot phase them out until we have done the hard things contained in the report.
What happened to the prison industry concept? It was one of the more imaginative ideas developed by all committee members. Admittedly there has been some minor progress in terms of the study of this concept. I have not heard how much consultation has taken place with the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and various Canadian industries to ensure that prisoners are productive, that there is a large and massive sale of goods produced by convicts on the market so that prisoners could pay their own way, support their dependants and compensate their victims. It would provide them with opportunities to receive some training and achieve a sense of well-being until they are released. One should make no mistake. There are very few people who will
February 6, 1979

not be back among the public. I have not heard much about such consultation.
In conclusion, I should like to make some comments in support of what was said by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) concerning the frustrations of the committee system. From time to time I have sat on both the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence and the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. I am disappointed that we in the House have not been able to use our committee system more effectively. Because of the fine work of the committee chairman, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan), I thought we were making a very interesting beginning. I thought we would be able to say that members of parliament do not sit and think about votes every minute of the day. I thought they could actually sit down and say that we have a national problem. We have identified it, we have seen it. I thought members would agree that we would solve the problem rather than making any more. When a government receives this type of report, it is vitally important that it be taken seriously and adopted. I cannot say that all 65 recommendations should be adopted, but surely the major and key recommendations should be.
When that has been accomplished, we will have gone a long way toward improving the committee system, the House and the manner in which members of parliament can make some positive contribution to the people of the country in general and their own constituents.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:

Of course, I am pleased this motion will be concurred in by the government. I would like the Solicitor General to take an opportunity, as quickly as possible, to specify what the government has agreed to in terms of the new reference. Since the government has adopted the motion of the hon. member for St. John's East, the committee should have no less a mandate than was given to the other subcommittee studying the penitentiary system. I agree there must be a limited time frame, but at least we will have an opportunity to examine the institutions again and see whether there has been any meaningful change.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few comments on the motion introduced by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt).
First of all, I congratulate the Solicitor General for his good words. He tried to encourage members of the opposition, saying in particular he wanted to see us be non-partisan. I think we have always worked in a non-partisan way in the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs and I am glad to see he recognizes that we want to be non-partisan.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is intelligent.
Concurrence in Committee Report

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Intelligence comes with non-partisanship.
What I note in the speech made by the Solicitor General is that he says he is prepared to force the officials of his department-he did not quite put it that way but I think that is what he meant-to force the officials of his department to set the main recommendations of the subcommittee on justice and legal affairs in motion. Again I congratulate him but what strikes me is that the only thing new right now is that they want to build other institutions. It seems to me the committee had recommended improving first what is working now in existing institutions-of course, things are going bad in some institutions.
I want to point out two things. First I think that for things to work well in institutions the number of inmates in each should not be increased from 250 to 400 as was recently decided because the committee determined that in an institution where you have 400 inmates it is very difficult to distinguish between those who want to help and better themselves and those who do not.
It is also difficult to separate the character differences of certain inmates. I therefore believe that the minister should consider suggesting to the Prison Guard Association that those who work within our institutions, and especially those who have direct contact with the inmates, not be entitled to belong to a union. In my opinion, as soon as there is a strong union within an institution, the union leaders, which include the president, the secretary and the executive, have a tendency to hide the little things that some of their colleagues can do to upset an inmate whom they do not like very much or whose looks they do not like, and so on. This was proven when we visited penal institutions. To insult an inmate, a guard may doodle on his letters or appear to be opening it or throwing it away, and so on. In my opinion, it is very frustrating for an inmate when a guard whom he must see every day does things like that.
I also believe that we should not spend one more dollar in our penal institutions without solving existing problems. We should also consider providing more reasonable wages for the inmate who wants to help himself. We should also, as recommended in the report, think about visiting rights and about making the prison system more humane by allowing visits for the wife of the inmate, his children, and so on, but in areas where the inmate and his wife and children could be left alone without being watched through a window, when the inmate has shown for example that he wants to amend his ways and become a full-part citizen after paying back society by serving his sentence.
I believe also that we should separate the inmates according to their age in present institutions. At this time, young people of 17, 18 or 19 are not comfortable when they are thrown in with 30, 40 or 50-year-old tough guys or hardened criminals. This is not their place, it is not their way of life. There are some who do not really mind and there is nothing we can do

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report for them, but as for the young people who are put in prison because of an unfortunate mistake or a drug charge-and I am not trying to excuse them, Mr. Speaker-I would like these inmates to have a chance to improve themselves and not be placed in permanent contact with hardened criminals or people who always lived outside the law or are always in trouble. As a matter of fact, they are always the ones to write to us.
We get dozens of letters, often from those who do not want to mend their ways. Those who do tell us either that they have been molested by a guard, or that the letter they sent out were opened, because they are being blackmailed; I feel we must absolutely improve that situation.
As for the committee, the minister is right in saying that it should look into the matter of the incarceration of children, the whole penal system for juvenile delinquents. In that regard, the study should also include what is shown on the state television network, in its various forms, whether it be films or stories which often are amoral, if not immoral as far as our children are concerned.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to recommend first that the possibility be looked into of changing the status of our prison guards. If it were to correspond to that of the members of the RCMP or private police agents, the well-being of our prisoners would be improved. To my mind, that would be a great step forward.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT TAKEOVER OF NORDAIR
speechtext:
1. The figure of
$28.4 million is composed of the following elements:
($Millions)
Price to be paid by Air Canada for the purchase of the outstanding shares of Nordair, plus or minus Nordair's after tax earnings or losses for the period commencing June 1, 1978.	$27.4
Air Canada's estimated out-of-pocket expenses.	1.0

2. The valuation methods used by Air Canada to determine a fair and reasonable price per share for all outstanding common stock of Nordair Ltd. at an anticipated takeover date of June 30, 1978 were as follows:
Order Paper Questions
(a)	The basic valuation method used was the replacement cost method. Under this method, Nordair was considered as a going-concern with its property and equipment being valued at replacement cost. Furthermore, all intangibles were eliminated and long-term obligations for leased aircraft were recognized. The estimated after tax profit for the first six months of 1978 was added.
(b)	Another test was made with a capitalization of earnings method under which the average of actual 1977 earnings results plus budgeted 1978 earnings results was multiplied by a reasonable earnings capitalization factor.
(c)	A final test was made with a discounted cash flow method under which future years estimated cash flows and residual values of assets were discounted at various reasonable rates of return.
(d)	The value of Nordair shares determined under the foregoing methods was tested with a liquidation valuation. All property and equipment were deemed disposed of at replacement cost with due consideration given to income taxes payable on recapture of capital cost allowance.
(e)	The basic valuation method used, supported by the other tests described, indicated a value per share within a narrow range of reasonableness.
(f)	External valuation consultants were asked to review in detail Air Canada's valuations. In their opinion, a reasonable basis, appropriate to the purpose and circumstances, and the principles and methods employed were in accordance with generally accepted valuation techniques.
3.	The $28.4 million includes an amount of $1 million for out-of-pocket expenses (see 1 above).
4.	These represent Air Canada's estimated costs associated with the acquisition of the outstanding shares of Nordair and include provision for:
(a)	Fees for evaluators (valuation of assets and shares of Nordair).
(b)	Fees and expenses in preparation for and attendance at hearings before the Canadian Transport Commission.
(c)	Legal fees.
(d)	Dealer fees.
(e)	Depository fees (deposit of shares in trust).
(f)	Printing costs (printing of offer).

speakeroldname: Mr. F. Oberle (Prince George-Peace River) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
that Bill C-410, to amend the Canada Labour Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I first of all thank hon. members in the House, specifically the House leader for the NDP, for accommodating me in allowing the substitution of Bill C-410 for Bill C-213 as listed on the order paper. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) did speak in response to the subject matter of this bill the last time I brought it to the attention of the House, sometime in 1977. He said at that time he would not even extend me the courtesy of thanking me for bringing the matter before the House so it might be debated. I realize it is quite a concession he is making today, therefore, and I thank him heartily for it.
It is not the first time that I have brought this matter before the House, but I have little reason to believe that hon. members will grant the necessary consent today to allow this bill to proceed further, and this will probably not be the last time I will discuss this bill in the House. I am reminded of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who repeatedly rises in this House to talk about matters very dear to his heart. I can certainly make the commitment that I shall debate this matter until such time as more of my colleagues in the House and more people in the areas concerned with industrial relations in our country adopt a more enlightened view so that parliament can act.
My bill in general deals with the rights of individual workers. I refer, of course, to all workers in the country, numbering approximately ten million; but I am more concerned with the members of our labour force who are organized, which is roughly one third of the work force and amounts to 3.2 million men and women. Strangely enough, as one examines this what I call elite group in our work force, one finds that they either work for the government in Crown corporations, where they are compelled to belong to a union, or they work for large corporations. I am referring to the particular corporations which have managed to insulate themselves from the harsh realities of the free market system and which simply pass on the costs of whatever they produce to the consumer. Some of them are offshore consumers and some of them are within our own country. The government's situation, of course, is that if
February 6, 1979

the cost of labour increases it is simply passed on to the taxpayer. There is no great concern among such employers as to how high the demand for additional wages or additional fringe benefits goes.
I have often asked myself, what is so bad about unions that they must compel members to belong? I know that many members of unions have asked themselves the same question: "Why do I have to be compelled to belong to my union?". I draw my experience from studies which I have made of other labour models throughout the world. I find in looking at our own labour relations model that there are some very serious discrepancies and anomalies.
Having spoken several times on this matter and having brought it forth on other occasions in the House, I have had an opportunity to answer some of the criticisms of the bill that have been voiced. The last time my bill was discussed in the House was in 1977, and at that time hon. members were glad to accept it, with the exception of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who said that he wished to have it disposed of as quickly as possible to get it out of here. I respect the hon. member's views in that regard, but the other hon. members who spoke said it was important that this matter be brought before the House for debate because it is a crucial issue and because in this regard we face a crisis in our country.
There are pressures on many hon. members from their constituents and the unions in this regard, and it is a good thing that this bill is being debated again so that hon. members may air their concerns and the concerns of their constituents and we may take a very serious look at the direction of industrial relations in our country. I am assuming, of course, that some of my misguided friends in my own constituency, who have chosen to misinterpret and misunderstand this bill, as have some members of the NDP, will not, once again, fight me on my position in the next election.
Bill C-410 which I introduced in this House for the first time in 1974 has been deliberately misnamed and misinterpreted by some people. The legislation adopted in the United States, which is similar to what I am proposing, is called the right to work legislation. I would prefer to call my bill freedom of association legislation. I think this title is rather appropriate because of the many things which are being said today about constitutional reform and the need to entrench in the constitution our commitment to certain fundamental democratic principles.
Much is said about the freedom and rights of the individual. The cardinal principle of democracy is freedom of association, individual rights and collective rights. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the present time is encouraging hon. members to give serious consideration to entrenching certain of these rights I have mentioned in the constitution. To what extent, however, does the freedom of the individual have to yield to the collective rights of groups?
The Task Force on Canadian Unity has made certain references in their assessment of these freedoms. The freedoms which they propose to entrench in the constitution are broken down into several categories and are indicated on page 107 of
Canada Labour Code
the report. First of all, they say that the right of the individual is paramount. This, of course, is the basis of the political parties represented in this House. The second category embraces the rights of people as individuals within particular groups. The third category covers the collective rights which can be exercised by a group, such as the right of unions to bargain. I have often wondered how far the collective rights of these groups should be allowed to proceed, particularly if they violate the rights or interests of individual Canadians.
The report goes on to discuss the collective rights of groups with a slant toward the right of the Francophone majority in the province of Quebec and the Francophone minorities in other parts of the country to speak their language. I appreciate that collective right and I respect it, but I cannot help but wonder if it could in some instances be taken to the point where a minority language group says, "Look, you are not giving us our way, we don't like you any more, we are going to leave the country". This situation could also apply to unions where they decide, because they are not getting their way at the bargaining table, not only to withdraw their essential service but to opt out of the country, regardless of what that means to the individual rights of Canadians. They say, "We are opting out. We are paralysing the country regardless of what it means to the individual rights of other Canadians. We have that additional power". I wonder just what authority, what forum, will make the final decision on how far these collective rights can be taken.
It is also advantageous to repeat such a debate as this in this House because it gives me an opportunity to answer some of the criticisms levelled against the bill the last time it was debated. I said I based my assessment of the situation on certain models. I have studied particularly the West German model. The criticism has been made that because of the behaviourial attitudes of different cultural backgrounds and different attitudes toward work, one cannot transpose that kind of model on the situation in Canada. If it cannot be transposed on the situation in Canada, can it be transposed on the situation in Great Britain? As you know, Mr. Speaker, many of the principles and traditions we have in Canada are inherited from Great Britain. They were inherited along with the British parliamentary system. Surely it can be said that the average worker in Great Britain has as deep a heritage as has the German worker.
The fact is, however, that the German constitution is somewhat different. It is not an accident that the West German models are somewhat different. Their constitution is only 25 or 27 years old, the most modern constitution in the free world. There are, of course, constitutional guidelines that restrict that particular freedom I have talked about if it offends or injures the freedom of the individual.
The basic principle that is being respected-and this is the crux of the problem in our country-is the freedom of association which my bill intends to restore. Freedom of association, which is one of the great cardinal principles of democracy, is

February 6, 1979
Canada Labour Code
interpreted differently in West Germany than it is in this country and in Great Britain. The worker is free to associate. As a matter of fact, in West Germany he has to have the opportunity to join a union, which workers in this country do not have and which I say they should have. In Germany, they cannot be compelled to join. The freedom of association is interpreted both ways: they are free to associate but cannot be compelled to associate.
If we are addressing ourselves to fundamental changes in our constitution, that is one of the changes that has to be entrenched-restoration of this cardinal principle of democracy, freedom of choice.
One of the arguments that has traditionally been made and was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the last time the bill was debated is to the effect that "Because I am not a Liberal and I do not agree with everything this government does, I should not have to pay taxes." That precisely underlines the argument I have advanced. The union power in this country puts itself on an equal footing with the power of this institution and the power of government. It says, "If I do not agree with what the government is doing, I do not have to pay taxes." At the same time it says: "I have a right to bargain. The right of the worker in an industry is that if he does not like what the union does he should not have to pay dues".
That is what I am saying. If they want to preserve a right that is equal to the institution of parliament, the institution of government, I say that is wrong. It points out precisely the problems we have in this country where the union exercises greater power than we exercise in parliament.
We have an instance at the moment where a union connected with the post office decided to disobey the law of the land. Members of that union will be reprimanded and may well lose their jobs in the public service because they chose to respect the law of the land and ignore a direction from their leadership to stay out when an order was made in this House for them to return to work. This is very dangerous, Mr. Speaker. It borders on anarchy and surely that is something we cannot tolerate in a free and great society such as ours.
The traditional argument is also that unions need protection to safeguard them against exploitation from corporate giants and unscrupulous employers. That is an age-old argument. There is no doubt that there is a need for unions. There was a need for unions when Mr. Justice Rand intervened in the Ford strike and gave unions the right to a closed union shop in the first place.
Times have changed, Mr. Speaker. Technology is light years ahead of the contemporary union structure in our country. We have a very good grip of, and very good control over, the behaviour of unscrupulous businessmen and corporations in this country so that that great fear no longer exists.
What we forgot as we modernized our industrial plant and integrated into it the technology that became available was that we are no longer competitive. We should have modernized as did the countries with whom we compete in world markets.

As they modernized their industrial relations process, so should we.
We are no longer competitive in world markets because of some of the difficulties the unions have created. I am not referring to wages, Mr. Speaker. I agree that some sectors of the economy are underpaid today. Some are overpaid, and traditionally they are always the ones that are unionized and we know that employers simply pass the cost on to the consumer or the taxpayer.
I am saying that because of irresponsible action we have not been able to get our products to market. We have had transportation systems shut down. The post office service has been interrupted. We seem to sit here and accept that it now takes up to ten days for a letter to come from Vancouver, British Columbia to Ottawa, when a few years ago it used to take three or four days.
It is time all that changed, Mr. Speaker. We must modernize our system of dealing with employers and workers and adopt an approach which other countries have found to be beneficial. If we do not, we will go the same route as Great Britain where there is a serious crisis. As we hear in daily news reports, it is impossible even for the Labour government to talk with the unions in a manner which is in the legitimate interest of the country as a whole.
We should not allow ourselves to be forced down this road, Mr. Speaker. Now is time for change. It is time for this bill to be taken to committee, for it to be debated in public, for the public to have their say, for union members to have their say. It is time for that two thirds of our work force to have access to a union and for the small businessmen to enter the debate that is carried on in parliament, in the board rooms of the nation and in the tripartite forum we are trying to establish. All these people have a right to be heard, and that is why I commend this bill to the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just happened to hear the hon. member say this is not a "right to work bill", that it is a "freedom of association bill". I think a rose by any other name would smell exactly the same way. If I were to give this bill a title it would be called "The Sting".
The hon. member talked a lot about freedom-freedom to associate, etc. I wonder where the Tory party labour critic is, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser). Indeed, where is the whole Tory party? Where have all the Tories gone? It is important for the workers in this country to hear the Conservative party position being put forward by the small entrepreneur from British Columbia, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). It is important to hear him put forward this so-called enlightened view of industrial relations in Canada in 1979.
It is nothing but a pile of hogwash! It is "right to work" legislation. Let us call it by its real name, "right to work." Let us also understand that "right to work" has nothing at all to do with creating employment. It has to do with union busting.
February 6, 1979

That is what the small entrepreneur, the so-called small businessman, this sawmill operator from British Columbia, is really talking about-busting the trade union movement. Fie wants to deny the workers the right to collective bargaining and the right to the union shop. That is what he is talking about, and that is not new, Mr. Speaker. He is not proposing anything new.
This goes back to 1935 when the Automobile Manufacturers Association got together to fight the Wagner act which gave the workers in the automotive industry the right to collective bargaining and the right to a union shop. He wants to go "forward into the past;" that is what the hon. member wants to do. He does not want to go forward with any new, decisive, dynamic industrial relations proposals; he wants to take us back with his Progressive Conservative party views to 1935.
It seems that the malaise of this right to work, which has now infected 20 southern states in the United States, has moved in to of all places the province of British Columbia. It was in 1975 that their founding meeting was held in Trail, B.C. It was made up of independent contractors and a businessmen's association. Incidentally, Phil Gagliardi, "flying Phil," was a key speaker along with Ralph Purdy. Ralph Purdy was the organizer of the right to work movement in the United States. Mr. Purdy happens to be a great John Bircher. He was there telling Canadian entrepreneurs how to handle the working class in this country.
What does this legislation mean?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Was Oberle there?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: I suspect the hon. member was there. As a matter of fact, it might be a conflict of interest for him to grind his axe in this House of Commons on his pet project. But what does this legislation mean? When one strips it of all the verbosity which the hon. member has put forward here this afternoon and, equates his crusade for union busting with the crusade of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for the poor and pensioned people of this country, it is like comparing Satan with something saintly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: The holy ghost.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
But what does it mean? What does it say? It says the corporations will have greater opportunity to put more profit in their pockets. Having torn down the workers' collectives and unions, each employer would then be free to work out an individual pay or wage scale with each worker. Can you imagine that in the work place, Mr. Speaker? Can you imagine each worker working out separately with his employer what he is going to get? Can you see that being healthy for the working environment? Can you see the old British mentality of divide and conquer in all its full glory in effect in the work place? The hon. member calls that modern industrial relations. We had that in the teaching profession in Ontario as far as I can remember. In effect, teachers agreed to move away from that situation because it depressed living and working standards.
Canada Labour Code
What does this legislation mean apart from allowing the corporations, and small entrepreneurs, to put bigger profits in their pockets? It means safety and health rules can be avoided. As each worker becomes concerned about his own job security, he would not complain about environmental security. He would not be concerned about the health hazards in the working place. The situation will be every man for himself. Whoever kisses the boss' toes the most are the ones whose jobs will be protected. That is what the hon. member calls modern industrial relations. That is what the Progressive Conservative party is offering to the working class of Canada as an alternative. The hon. member should be ashamed of himself.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: We experienced that in the Sudbury basin, Mr. Speaker. We all remember what it was like before the unions came into the Sudbury basin in 1943. We remember when there was no union. We had a right to work then and all the workers would be lined up. The foreman would come out and he would say, "Today, you have a job". Then to the next person he said, "You have a job", and so on. He would then say, "The rest of you can go home". To keep their jobs men would allow the bosses to sleep with their wives. The men had to bring chickens as well. There was a chicken in every foreman's pot, but none in the worker's pot.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: That is Oberle's policy. It is PC policy.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: That is the Progressive Conservatives for you. Is that their charter for industrial relations? I think it is shameful, Mr. Speaker, totally shameful.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: No wonder the people of Canada are laughing.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
It is the unified, collective strength in the working place that has improved health and safety conditions. Anyone who knows anything about collective bargaining knows of the strides and improvements which have been made because workers have collectively bargained to improve the environment in the working place.
What else does this legislation do? This bill would give a totally free hand to the employer in the matter of hiring and firing. The potential for abuse is evident. Once the freedom is there it is abused. We see it in the banks today. I know banks that have hired flashy young men, posted them to a branch, and their job is to find out which young women in their branch are organizing a union. A man comes in as an assistant accountant. He takes out the young women and wines and dines them in an effort to find out who is organizing the union. The minute this information is secured these people are fired. The record of the Labour Relations Board in its various judgments against the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce gives examples. But like the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River, they all believe in the right to work and will do anything to prevent the organization of collectives in the work place.

February 6, 1979
Canada Labour Code
What else would this bill do? It would depress the standard of living of the working class in this country. Anyone who knows the history of the trade union movement in Canada knows that it has done more as a single force to improve the standard of living and the quality of life for the workers of this country. I say again that anyone who knows anything about the trade union movement knows that that has been so. Employers have not been willing to improve these things. Lives have been lost in the process of trying to improve the work place and the workers' standard of living. For example, in northern Ontario people in the bush have lost their lives when organizing the woodworkers unions. We know it from the strikes and the sacrifices that have been made by workers as they fight, not to get from generous employers what they feel they should get, but to get what is their right to live on a decent wage in order to provide for their families some dignity. What else does this bill do? It undermines the democratic process. A union is a very democratic organization.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING FREEDOM OF ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
They vote. If the majority of workers vote to recognize a certain union as representing them, the majority wins, and you cannot have the minority going off and doing its own thing. Oh, they would love to have all the benefits of the union. The hon. member's bill would allow this. Let us get back to the title of this bill. It should be called right to work legislation. I, and I am sure many members of my party, are opposed to it for a very basic reason, and that is that it would create nothing but confrontation between employer and employee. I agree that there are many things to be desired of the union movement. One of the things I find most irksome is the closed shop. Valued, experienced and skilled workmen in my riding have been denied the opportunity to work at jobs down the street from their residences because of the closed shop constraint. One of the worst offenders was the Rock and Tunnel Workers Union No. 1, which never even bothered to reply to my telephone calls or letters.
Finally, I asked Bill King, then the minister of labour of British Columbia, what was going on with that union. I asked why the union did not reply to its mail or take into consideration the employment rate in Kootenay West. The minister of labour of British Columbia replied to me that he agreed with me, that he wished he could help me, that he was sorry but that he could not interfere. There was an abuse of the union system.
On the other side of the coin, let us consider the example in the United States which is often quoted and abused. There is right to work legislation in 20 states. What are those states? They are nearly all agricultural, they are not industrial. There are five states in the United States which, since 1947, have repealed the right to work legislation. We find three things in these states in the U.S. First, they are principally agricultural; they are less industrialized, less unionized, and they pay the lowest wages. One can accurately state that these three factors were important factors in shaping the political climate since those laws were introduced.
There is no need for me to continue speaking on this subject. I could make a 20-minute speech and I could make a one-hour speech. I simply want to go on record as saying that there are many other ways in which we can accomplish an understanding between union and management, and those ways are by negotiation. I go on record as saying that there are many ills

and many irresponsible actions carried out by both the employers and the employees, by unions and by management. I saw a classic example of it in downtown Trail where some elements of the labour movement, when we had a civic workers' strike, decided that that was the right time to scatter garbage all over the main streets of Trail.
That day the announcer said, "Folks, that big labour demonstration in downtown Trail is over now, but some of the irresponsible elements have scattered garbage all over the streets," or something to that effect. That strike had been going on for months. Do you know what happened? That was the only statement on the radio, but how stupid those people looked, how irresponsible they appeared when the citizens of Trail, the children, the high school students, and the housewives and the workers, came down and cleaned the streets of Trail without being solicited to do so. They were showing to the people of B.C. and the rest of Canada that they are proud of their community and that no irresponsible idiots will label them as being people who do not care about their community. The streets were cleaner than they had been for months.
You can look at the other side of the coin too. I know there is another member who wishes to speak on this subject and I would like to give him that opportunity, so, although I would like to continue speaking on this point, I will bow to my friend across the way.

1 had high hopes for this report because we took a non-partisan approach to a national problem of crisis proportions. I am not one of those who have been critical of the penitentiary services, or of the ministry of the Solicitor General for what has been done. Indeed, some of the recommendations have been implemented. My grievance, and it is shared unanimously by all members of that subcommittee on the penitentiary system, is not in connection with what the department of the Solicitor General has done, but with what it has not done. We unanimously agreed, Liberals, Conservatives, members of the

We were also unanimous in the belief that one of the main ills of the system was the correctional personnel themselves, and that the quickest way to cure the ills which existed with respect to that one third segment of the civil service in the system was to create a force entirely independent of the public service which would be structured and administered along the same line as the RCMP.

That is precisely why the recommendation was made. It was not made to deprive them of any union benefits but to get them away from the effect of unionism on the service itself, and to replace it with something else. That something else is a system which is working admirably well in the RCMP. The members of that force are not in a union. They do not belong to the PSAC, but they have a system of employee representation which is very effective. The same matters which are considered by the PSAC with respect to personnel in the penitentiary system are effectively dealt with by a system in the RCMP which is not part of the PSAC. I can tell him also, and I believe that it was a general consensus among committee members, that the reason for the unrest which had reached a peak when the committee commenced its examinations of the penitentiary system would again surface. Perhaps it was by way of exhaustion, but certainly it was as a result of the narrowing in each case of what was being attempted to be done that it was generally found to be acceptable by other members of the committee.
Of course, there is what 1 would call the subterranean relevance, and I do not use this term pejoratively with respect to the hon. member for St. John's East. This point was illustrated by him when he talked about the deep feeling in the committee that there was not much point in having any reference if nothing was being done about the previous one. This is the kind of thing which very much occupies the minds and feelings of members of parliament in committees. 1 believe there are several reasons why the motion is in order if that question should come up again.
One thought which struck me at the time, and it strikes me again now, was that the motion gives priority of place and puts most stress on the question that is already before the com-mitee-the question of the rights of children. In placing first the question of the incarceration of children and then in talking about the penal system, it again puts children before adults.
More important than that, there is a continuity in concept and in needs in the whole notion of incarceration. It is very difficult to draw a line. In our viewings of the penitentiaries we found, for instance, on at least one occasion a prisoner who

had been in federal penitentiary at age 16. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) said, we had been having great difficulty with the reference on children's rights in finding out exactly where the age of a child, as encompassed by that subject matter and by the needs of the situation, could be drawn. We saw the matter in continuity and it was for this reason, among others, that we felt the motion was in order.
I think we would all acknowledge the sentiments that were expressed at that time by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham when he said, as reported at page 33 of volume No. 8 of the report of the proceedings of the committee:
The purpose, quite frankly is to enlarge the terms of reference so that we can talk about penitentiaries and the penal system in general and not just the penal system as it refers to the incarceration of children.
That was certainly the motivation of the members of the committee and it would be folly to deny it here. But it is not that which is incorporated in the words of the motion, and I think the motion as formally presented is in order.
Having made that case for relevance, I should like to do what others who have spoken in the debate have done- disregard relevance entirely and speak on the aspect of this problem which the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) devoted all of his time to, and that is the penitentiary system. I would say that the penitentiary system has been improving steadily in Canada since the report of the subcommittee in June, 1977. Although it has been improving steadily it has been at a very disappointing pace, and with very disappointing limitations.
I think we would not be having a debate if it were only a question of the pace of implementation. We all know, as politicians, that things usually take longer than we would wish, and sometimes longer than seems possible. What we are concerned about are the limitations which the Solicitor General and the penitentiary service seem to impose on the recommendations we made. Because of the time I have, I am only going to comment on two kinds of questions. One of those has to do with the size of penitentiaries and the other has to do with recommendation No. 26, and, in particular, the comments of the Solicitor General about that and his apparent understanding of it.
First of all, with respect to the question of the larger size of institutions which the government has recently announced, the Solicitor General said this afternoon that there was no solid evidence that smaller-sized institutions would do more for prisoners. I think we should be frank, Mr. Speaker, and admit there is a certain skepticism on the part of listeners that a doctrine which had been accepted up to that point by the whole penitentiary service in Canada should be questioned and discarded at a time when there were perhaps financial pressures which caused the change. If the argument were put purely in terms of the government's restraint program it would be a little easier, but when it is given this veneer of rationalization it is perhaps not quite so easy to accept, and it leaves us with a somewhat uneasy feeling.
In the press conference which he gave on this subject, and presumably also reflecting the views of the Solicitor General,
February 6, 1979

the commissioner of corrections, Mr. Yeomans, is reported by the Globe and Mail on January 1, 1979, as having said:
Not one of those studies was based on any empirical data-
He said that of the earlier studies on which we relied, especially the famous Mohr report which was the foundation of our recommendation.
He went on to say:
Every one of those was an emotional study ... There isn't any evidence anywhere to support 200-man institutions.
Later the article continued:
Mr. Yeomans says studies this year by engineers and accountants found that the cost of running the smaller prisons, which were to be built over the next five years, would be 'enormously higher' than for larger ones.
Furthermore, he says, a sociological study of two medium-security prisons-a new one at Mission, B.C., that holds fewer than 200 men, and an older one at Warkworth in Ontario that holds 450-found no substantial difference.
'In fact, the advantage if any was slightly on the side of Warkworth because you could offer a greater variety of programs in the larger institutions.'
It would be very interesting for us to have those studies. I would invite the Solicitor General to allow the committee to see these documents so that we could see for ourselves whether the lack of solid evidence he refers to as the basis for our recommendation might also extend perhaps to his decision. While I am inviting him today to table that document so that we can see it, perhaps he would also let us see Dr. Boyd's report on the application of social therapy to institutions in Canada.
This is an especially important matter in the context of the size of institutions because if social therapy were to work, prisons would have to be built in the form of 30-person units, perhaps, which are entirely self-contained for every purpose- for work, recreation, and everything else. The system could not operate in any other way. If that were to be the future course of the penitentiary system we should obviously know that as soon as possible, especially before we build any more expensive institutions. It is very important that we on the standing committee see this document as early as possible, as well as the documents on which the Solicitor General is relying for the change in policy that he has made.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Good, good.

Perhaps it might be thought that there are no really hard monetary consequences attaching to the decision on size except favourable ones. I might point out that in the package of announcements the Solicitor General made about the size of institutions, he announced one which was very surprising to members of the committee, that is, that the Kingston penitentiary would be restored for business and that Millhaven, which until now had been the maximum security institution in Ontario, would be downgraded to a medium security institution. Perhaps he might consider inviting Monica Dickens, who is the great great grand-niece of Charles Dickens, who was there for the opening in 1835, to attend the reopening in 1980 or 1981 of the new Kingston penitentiary. The cost is to be $33 million, of which $27 million is to restore Kingston to its former glory as the maximum security institu-
Concurrence in Committee Report
tion, and $6 million to downgrade Millhaven from its present status to a medium security institution.
The consequences of the government's policies are not always a saving of money, and it is very hard to understand in a document which is otherwise directed toward saving government expenditures that there would be a recommendation of this kind. I shall make a suggestion in a moment about why I think that decision was made.
The other matter to which I wish to turn briefly now is recommendation No. 26. We made this recommendation for an entirely independent penitentiary service because, in looking at the penitentiaries as they are in Canada today, we realized there was no other way the government would ever get control of them. We could hardly expect to control inmates if we cannot control those who are supposedly guarding and instructing them.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The Solicitor General says we have not thought this recommendation through, especially its effect on the unions. I wondered, in listening to some of his comments, whether he has read through the text which accompanies our recommendations. Looking at the recommendation apart from the text, one does not get the full flavour. I want to read into the record a number of points on which some misunderstanding has been expressed.
At page 80 of the report it says:
We find a high level of agreement on the point that a union is not inconsistent with correctional work with respect to wages and fringe benefits.
At page 81 it says:
-since... the Service should resemble a police force in its discipline and professionalism, employees might well wish to have their interests represented, not by a union, but by an association like that existing in the RCM Police. This should be decided by the employees themselves by secret ballot.
The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has talked about the advantages of having an association of that kind, and I recognize the advantages are considerable. But, Mr. Speaker, we did not recommend against having a union, and there is considerable misunderstanding on this point. This is an open choice for the employees to make, and I want to make sure the government understands that. As a matter of fact I would find it hard to imagine that the employees would not vote to continue some form of union. That is perfectly within our contemplation. That is their decision to make, not ours, but that union should have some limitations. It should not have the right to strike. It should have a code of discipline and means of enforcing that discipline which could, for the first time, bring about effective discipline within the penitentiaries. It should also be able to have a professionalism which we think would not otherwise be possible.
The Solicitor General, in his choices with respect to the areas covered by recommendation No. 26, does not even go as far as the interdepartmental working group which his predecessor set up. They made recommendations. But with respect

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report to the adjudication of grievances, the Solicitor General says that we should retain the present method, the one which the penitentiary management told us made it impossible to fire anyone, whatever the person had done. This was the one which we found totally unsatisfactory.
The Solicitor General reasons that his policy would be easier to accomplish and it would cause less confrontation. If ease of accomplishment, especially in terms of time, was the criterion-we are already nearing the end of two years from the time of our report-I think we might begin to ask why even that limited reform has not yet taken place. As the hon. member for Yukon has pointed out, in order to achieve anything we have to achieve certain fundamental things. We would prefer to wait, if necessary, another year or two to get the right kind of reform, rather than to settle for something now that is less than satisfactory.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
As far as confrontation is concerned, this problem can probably never be settled without some confrontation with some of the people in our penitentiaries at the present time. We should not seek confrontation, but we should not seek to avoid it either. We should establish the policies which we think we should have. I suggest that the reason we are downgrading Millhaven from a maximum to a medium institution now is that we have thrown in the sponge. We have said that we cannot get control of Millhaven. That is the reason we are spending $33 million to do something which, on the face of it, smacks of absurdity.
If one looks at the matter in those terms one can see that the difference between our proposal and that of the Solicitor General is not just some fanciful abstract one, it is one which is having harsh, concrete consequences at the moment.
My time is almost up, Mr. Speaker, but I will conclude with a few words from a letter which I received recently from an inmate. I presume my letter is from a different inmate than the one who wrote to the hon. member for New Westminster. For his own protection I do not want to reveal the person's name. This was a New Year's letter thanking me for what the committee had been trying to do. In part his letter reads:
After five years in this system I have never really felt fear whether at the B.C. pen during the riots or here.
The inmate is referring to Millhaven when he says "here." He goes on to say:
But for some reason I sit back now and in looking towards the new year, I feel a deep-set fear which I can't explain. I fear that this year will bring about a lot of pain and the ones that will take the blows will be eventually us. I saw desperation at the B.C. pen. and how it played with an inmate's mind. But here I see hatred. It is so bitter and deep that you could cut it with a butter knife and not even penetrate the surface.
Perhaps that is a little better phrased than some of the comments I receive from inmates, but it is very similar to the comments I get in the 50 to 100 letters I receive each week from inmates in various institutions across the country. Our proposals were not written from the viewpoint of the inmates, but from the viewpoint of the public interest.
[Mr. MacGuigan.1
Sometimes this is a way of measuring how the system is working by observing the attitudes of consumers. I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for New Westminster, that it would be desirable for us to have a look at the institutions to see how the policies which we recommend, so many of which have been put in place as the Solicitor General tells us, are actually working in the institutions.
I wish I had time to deal with all the aspects of this. However, the important point is that I think the committee is unanimously dissatisfied with the way things are going. That is certainly the message I would like to leave tonight.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

And knowledge, absolutely correct.
I also want to congratulate my friend, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). All these people were members of the special committee who travelled across this country to examine what is going on in the institutions.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Do not forget the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt).

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, I certainly will not do that. He is always paying me compliments.

speechtext: Lawyers are all the same.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Some say lawyers are all the same. But I find that human behaviour and difference in personality in the legal profession exist there the same as in every other profession, even with those very strong union people.
I would like to take this opportunity to say that not only should we be looking at the conditions of the institutions, our prisons and penitentiaries, but we should be examining the
February 6, 1979

laws and the environment that got many of those people into those institutions. If John Howard, the prison reformer, were alive today perhaps he would want to see some of those institutions I have seen.
Although I was not a member of the special committee, I have visited institutions. As a lawyer of some years standing, I have seen many conditions under which people live. I have seen in this House of Commons people who believe in reform and crusades, like myself in reference to the criminal code, bring in private members bills only to have them talked out. It has been done by all governments ever since I came here. The backbenchers are practically hired to talk out bills.
I think that when we are talking about children, and when we have a Criminal Code as archaic as the law set out in sections 12 and 13 of that Code, it is certainly time for amendment. Take this, for example:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was under the age of seven years.
Seven years! So if he is seven and a half years old and throws a can of tomatoes at a stepfather who has been brutalizing him-

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will give an example in a few minutes of a case in which a child was found guilty of manslaughter at nine years of age, and sentenced to imprisonment in one of our penitentiaries. This happened since I came to this House, yet I cannot get the government to act. For ten long years I have asked in private members' bills to have the age of responsibility raised. Nothing has been done, yet we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who talks about civil rights in glowing terms.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Would you permit a question?

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, I do not have time. I have only 20 minutes in which to make my speech. Let the hon. member make one-he has had lots of opportunities. I will give another example of what I mean:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was seven years of age or more, but under the age of fourteen years, unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and appreciate that it was wrong.
The age limit set out in those two sections should be raised. Over a long period I have continually asked that this be done. Such action in itself would remedy the situation I have described. In the sixties I raised in this House the situation of a boy called Henri, written up by Mr. Bill Trent of Weekend Magazine at that time. He got the information from Mr. MacLeod of the penitentiary service. This boy was put into one of our penitentiaries in New Brunswick, and he was so small that after they had locked him up in solitary confinement for the night he was able to creep through the bars. The guards, the enforcement officers-I can get emotional about this having been a defence lawyer all my life-took up a collection
Concurrence in Committee Report so that he could have a bicycle to ride around the prison yard during the daytime.
Take a look at what is still going on. These figures are for 1977. Five of the inmates of penitentiaries are under the age of 16, 38 are under the age of 17, 1,343 are between the ages of 18 and 21. What is wrong with the system of law in this country and with the administration of justice that we should be incarcerating more people per capita in different institutions here than any western nation? I might even be critical of the judiciary. It seems to me the belief is held that unless you hand out between five and ten years you don't think you are punishing anyone.
I will make a prediction. We abolished capital punishment and set a penalty of 25 years for first degree murder, without right to parole unless granted after 15 years by a judge. I predict that within five years, at the rate murder is increasing in this country, 800 people will have been found guilty of first degree murder, some of them for the second and third time in the penitentiaries. Are they to be placed in with children? Are they to be segregated? What have they got to lose if they take the life of a law enforcement officer? Nothing.
Look at the figure for Ontario-I could not get the figures for another province. In the training institutions which are really children's prisons and jails-there is no difference- there is one child under the age of nine, there are five under the age of ten, there are ten under the age of 11, there are 25 under the age of 12, 17 under the age of 13, 204 under the age of 14, 384 under the age of 15, and 34 under the age of 16.
Take the case of a fellow by the name of Tony, now 23, serving three years in Collins Bay Penitentiary for armed robbery. He was mistreated by his stepfather, never given anything-if he wanted something he had to steal. He was caught for truancy at the age of 13 and sentenced to a training school for three years. He was small for his age, weighing only 75 pounds. The discipline at the school was extremely rigorous; he was repeatedly beaten by the staff and by fellow inmates. His wrists were so small that when they arrested him the last time the handcuffs fell off his wrists. These are facts which I have discovered through research.
Consider the case of Peter, aged 35, serving a five-year sentence for assault causing bodily harm. When he was a child his parents broke up and he was sent to live with his 89-year-old grandmother. Children's Aid took him away and sent him to detention home for being a truant. One day, when he was 16, he broke a parking meter. He was caught and taken to Cobourg Training School in handcuffs. One of the instructors at the school beat him with his fists because he did not like his attitude. I could go on. 1 could put dozens and dozens of such cases on record.
As Pierre Berton said in an article he wrote on the subject, one by-product of all this is homosexuality, since young offenders are often dumped into prison compounds along with old and hardened men. It is almost axiomatic when young people are placed in such prisons, especially children as young as 13. I referred to this when I spoke in the sixties. Nowadays they are sent to what are called training centres. In my own

February 6, 1979
Concurrence in Committee Report
city of Calgary they have incarcerated kids. It is the same wherever you go.
Surely it is time for reform. I am proud to have belonged for a number of years to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, a non-partisan committee in which we are able to come to grips with many of these problems in the spirit of good will rather than in a partisan way. Those are the circumstances in which we get a speech like the one the chairman of the committee made this evening. We hear such speeches from all quarters of the House by members who are endeavouring to get the recommendations of the subcommittee approved. These members are asking for an extension of the time of the reference so that they can go back to these institutions and talk to those who are incarcerated, some of them in solitary confinement, in what they call the hole. We want to find out what improvement has taken place in the year which has passed since the committee travelled across the nation.
1 was glad to see that today the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) bent under pressure-his henchmen had earlier tried to get this motion ruled out of order. In my view, not nearly enough encouragement has been given to the committee. I say that surely, at a time when conditions are such that riot after riot is taking place-trouble and dissension are everywhere- the government should look once again at what is taking place in these institutions.
It is my philosophy that young people, when they come into this world, are like a piece of white paper with no writing on it. What happens to them along the trail of human life is often the result of factors in their environment. We are all a part of everyone we have met. Once a person is incarcerated it is a case of "out of sight, out of mind." That is why this debate is so important. That is why the committee, which did such an excellent job, much of it during the recess, travelled across the nation to examine at first hand the problems of these institutions.
I will make two points before I sit down. Let us get on with one of the great reforms of all time. In one of his articles Doug Fisher said that I am not a reformer. I do not know where he has been. I have introduced bill after bill, as the committee knows, to try to amend the Code. The Law Reform Commission should stop philosophizing and get down to redrafting the Criminal Code of Canada, which is 100 years old.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
