I could read section after section which does not apply to the modern world. Let us streamline the law and bring it into line with the eighties, but we will not do so with this worn out, dried up old prune of a government. This government has had it. We must get some new blood.
Sometimes we have to become partisan. I agree with the lady who interrupted me a moment ago that sometimes we have to become partisan. She herself does so in order to get her own party to move. The hon. member is a reformer. Other hon.

members opposite are not reformers, they are sitters. They like their jobs, their salaries, and their executive capabilities.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is nothing partisan about the truth.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I must agree with my House leader in that regard.
The second thing we must do is get our institutions in line with the eighties. We should set up family courts and bring in a young offenders law so that people will have a chance when they are brought before our justice system. There should not be the confrontation and the antagonistic system of criminal law we have now where defence counsel is against prosecutor, and where judges are against this person or that person. Young men and women should have a chance in this society of ours instead of ending up in institutions which are such a disgrace that even John Howard would have blushed if he had seen them.
That is my message in this debate. I hope it will penetrate the government, for whatever time it sits, and God help us if it sits much longer.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 20 months ago this committee was called on to serve its country at a time when our maximum security institutions were rocked by more riots, bloodshed, anger, pain, and cost to the taxpayer in two years than in all of the 42 preceding years. Twenty months ago in our first recommendation we wrote that "a crisis exists in the Canadian penitentiary system, that it could be met only by the immediate implementation of large-scale reforms and that it was imperative that the then solicitor general act immediately on the report as a matter of the utmost urgency." This month the status of recommendation No. 1 is that "the balance of this report is a statement of the actions to January, 1979, on the implementation of the recommendations in this report."
I say that the status is non-existent with regard to the state of crisis and tragedy which I know now exists. The implementation, for example, of what is called a special handling unit in Millhaven has become a basis for the continuing bullying, harassment and hoodlum activity of a few men who pretend to be leaders of a so-called union. I think that union exists to the disgrace of all of us who strongly believe in trade unionism.
I was a trade unionist. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt), the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and all of us on the penitentiary committee went to great pains to find a way not to ban or attack the union because of these horrible people. Because of these people there was havoc in the prisons and much damage and injury to inmates, as well as guards.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: You don't mean every local.

subsubtopic: CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, not every local. I am talking about Millhaven, and I am not talking about all the guards in the prison. The

union to which I refer did not represent the full staff-not all the guards or treatment people. It represented a handful of people who made sure that there was no representation at meetings.
Today we are going to rebuild Millhaven at a cost of $33 million. I say that it would be cheaper to implement our report, to fire those hoodlum leaders, and face the courts, if necessary, than it would be to rebuild a prison without Finding a solution to the tragedy of Millhaven and those who are inside. Both guards and inmates are victims of those few people. Guards are still Finding their tires slashed. They are still threatened at pubs. If they want to serve on a committee to help in rehabilitation, they face injury and suffering.
I am proud to intervene in this debate as a continuation of my duty as one of a non-partisan committee. It is remarkable that the hon. member for Yukon, the hon. member for New Westminster and all the members of the committee managed to sustain non-partisan standards right up to this time. One or two did come in latterly who created some change. I was very uneasy about trends towards partisanship instead of sincerity in this matter.
I am intervening for two basic reasons. The first is that the penitentiary committee should be given a reference so that it can return and check claims of new unrest and administrative wrongs. I, and perhaps others on the committee, suspect that things are being covered up by the word "implementation". I do not believe that the most important and crucial recommendations have been implemented-those that can save taxpayers money, eliminate useless and damaging bureaucracy, and eliminate control by a handful of hoodlum guards who will not even allow treatment programs to go ahead in some of our prisons. In fact, with regard to one of our most important recommendations, recommendation No. 26, there are 17 pages devoted to the pretence that there has been implementation with regard to the union. Those pages are a cover up with social worker terms as "discussions held", "selected, separate employees involved", "questions put", "analyses", "assessment of effectiveness", "review of reasons" and "consultation". Those words indicate there has been no action, just talk. At the end of all talk and at the end of all dreams, must be action.
As the hon. member for New Westminster noted, there was not one significant incident while our committee was working. I know that every member of the committee who gets letters and who goes to the prisons today asks inmates "please wait". We ask the guards not to get angry, and to stick it out. We ask them to, "please, please wait, don't blow it because we are still trying to work out the prison problems and implement the report."
I hope that does not give false hope. I know I write letters saying, "Keep it cool, the parliamentary committee is serious and honest." I am certain that is why there was minimum violence for a considerable time, even after one report was tabled. We did manage to keep the lid on because of our contacts.
The report of the penitentiary subcommittee is not bits and pieces. It is not the kind of report of which only small parts
Concurrence in Committee Report can be implemented with the expectation that the prison system can be improved and the lives of those inside can be restored.
The reference with regard to the bill which is before the committee now is relevant, because I can see that children's rights may very well be written in beautiful language, but that will not matter if we put children through a prison system which makes them more dangerous when they come out than when they went in.
The one thing society must worry about is protection of society. That is not done by cruel security. It is not done by locking men and women into cages for 23'/2 hours a day, by abusing them, gassing them and harassing them. This only guarantees they come out more dangerous than before. And 99 per cent of all those in prison do come out-they come out as of law, as of right. They walk beside us on the streets; they shop with us in the stores; they go to ballgames with us and sit beside us at hockey games. If they are more dangerous when they come out of the prison system, society is not served. Our report as a whole-not in bits and pieces-was designed to change the whole prison system, to assure the reformation of those committed to federal care.
Now, what are they doing? I suggest that the commissioner and his group of executives-that bureaucracy at the top-are not implementing our recommendations but rather are spending millions of dollars on task forces which travel all across Canada to find ways to avoid implementation. I see members of those task forces all the time on the planes. I hear them talking about how they have just done this job in a prison, and laugh about it. The task forces are redundant, they are repeating our work at the cost of millions of dollars to Canadians. I suggest they are not implementing our report but rather finding ways not to implement it. For example, the directors of prisons and of regions would not want the regional headquarters closed as our report recommended, because it would mean a loss of jobs at the top.
The second point I want to make which is so important- probably the most important reason for my rising to speak here tonight-is in regard to the whole system of committees of the House of Commons. Are we, members of committees, working long hours on these committees-sometimes on three committees a day, one committee meeting running into another-simply strutting and fretting on the stage as we are doing here, or are we there to serve the people of Canada? I suspect it has reached the stage where we rubber stamp budgets in our committees and the bureaucracy takes control from there.
It is similar in the CBC where we approve the budget and the executives, the officials, take the money and use it to pay Knowlton Nash $20 a minute, $90,000 a year; they use the rest to perpetuate people at the top, instead of for good programming. The same situation exists when we pass the solicitor general's budget; the money goes to the top bureaucracy. It does not go down to the treatment of the inmates, to

I say that unless a real study of the whole committee system is undertaken and reforms are brought in, we might as well not work in this House. The feeling that we waste time in our committees is proven by the fact that we were an all-party penitentiary subcommmittee and that this report was accepted unanimously in the House. There was no dissension on it. It could very well have been implemented, even including the very difficult problem of dealing with the union leaders and with the removal of regional headquarters.
Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that about eight years ago regional headquarters for all of western Canada, for the four western provinces, consisted of eight people in a mobile home on the prison compound of the B.C. penitentiary? Today it probably comprises 181 people, I do not have the exact figure. Twenty months ago we recommended that regional headquarters be eliminated. Possibly the most they should do is to monitor the prison and see that prisoners are supplied with things likes towels and toilet tissue. That is all it is worth. What has happened since our report was tabled? Regional headquarters were enlarged. This goes to prove that we are held in total contempt. The officials tell us that they are implementing our report in this regard. Well they have not cut, but added, a regional director general. All that means is we have another level in their bureaucracy, and our committee is held in total contempt, as is this House.
The partisan comments that have been made here about the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) disturb me very much because I feel that there was a genuine attempt to understand and implement the report by the previous solicitor general, who worked closely with us during our work and this has been continued by the present solicitor general. I am convinced that the bureaucracy in every department of government has become very strong, and I must say the opposition and the media make it impossible to clean up the mess.
For example, I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in one case why he did not fire a few people to show that parliament is the boss. He told me that when he fired one government employee the opposition tore him apart, the media tore him apart, and he was even brought before the courts. I say, "Fine, fire a few, go before the court, face the court, but let us not have this contemptuous approach to our system and to our whole democratic process."
I am serving notice in this House that I have a case right now that I intend to fight right here. Probably, Mr. Speaker, I am behaving quite improperly and I am not following the rules because I still am not fully acquainted with all the processes

here. It is the Faibish matter, that CRTC commissioner who behaved so contemptuously toward this member of parliament. It is not just the incident involving the threat to do something crude with a pin but the whole principle that if this public servant had been in private business he would have been fired for gross misconduct. But here he can stay, and probably be promoted! The same is happening in the prison system.
I say that if the Faibish salary is not cut to $1 in the estimates which will come before us in March,-as an example-then I will vote against the supply bill in the House. I do not see why we should automatically accept the fact that these people should get their salary and yet not behave with respect for the public and for members of parliament. This is exactly what has happened in the penitentiary service. The commissioner says he cannot keep in touch with the 50 prisons. I suggest they are not all in riot and there are only six maximum penitentiaries. If he cannot handle them, then he should either resign or be fired. That is one of the reasons why he will not implement our report.
I want to say, before I complete my statement, that if we can all work as we did in the committee, recognizing right from the start the fact that there is a crisis in our prison system, as well as recognizing the other crises in our society and working together as a unit, we will not be destroyed by the bureaucracy. We will not be divided, and our parliament conquered, split, and held in contempt across this country.
I want to say also that last week I brought out two points to the Solicitor General. One involved my concern over parole and the management of the parole system. I learned later that immediately he contacted the parole director and the parole board and has been working with them since. On Thursday I was out to dinner at the halfway house, the post release house of the John Howard Society here.
I discovered it had opened two months ago, but in that time there were only three people in it. We keep being told that there is a shortage of after care for the transition from penitentiaries into society of hard core prisoners. But here we have only three people; there is space for 14 people. I mentioned that to the Solicitor General and apparently the remedy has been started. So it is not fair to talk about politics and political neglect by the Solicitor General, because this is a big job which, I suppose, must be handled by officials. But the officials must be the servants, not the masters of the people and of the House.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure to participate in a debate such as this, particularly when one has been preceded by such fine speakers speaking with unanimity, having one common goal and, by and large, forsaking the concept of political partisanship.
I must admit I approached this debate with hesitancy, knowing this was going to take place since some time last week. I was concerned about what would result from the debate today so that, on my own initiative, I approached the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General (Mr. Young)
February 6, 1979

to express to him the fears I had about some adverse effects which this debate might have. At the same time, I spoke to the liaison official between us in the subcommittee on the penitentiaries and the commissioner. I see that Mr. Fife is here in the gallery tonight, I presume to carry back our thoughts to the commissioner.
I approached this day with hesitation because I thought there would probably be some adverse results from this debate which would further impede the success and the implementation of our prison report. 1 say this because, when I sat through the last meeting of our committee on justice and legal affairs, I sensed that a real problem might arise as a result of the feelings of the officials of the Canadian correctional services. There was no doubt in my mind that those officials felt that things were not going right so far as their relationship with the committee was concerned. I felt that myself, and I seized the opportunity to write to the commissioner about it. Indeed his reply to me confirmed what I had observed at that meeting.
The problem is the same one identified in the report of the subcommittee. The difficulty with the prisons is not a problem of bricks and mortar, it is a problem of people. The last time I sat in the Standing committee I saw a people's problem. In fact there were two adversary positions. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) very admirably described, there was the position of the public service. Perhaps the hon. member has put her finger on the most important problem, not only in the area we are discussing tonight but in the total area of government as I have seen it in the last four or five years I have been in Ottawa. One could feel the tension and failure to communicate between the two sides in committee. On the one side there was administration representing the Canadian correctional services, and parliamentarians on the other. When there are those types of adversary positions, we will not be successful.
When I realized that this debate was to take place today, I was concerned we would exacerbate the problem. I felt that the justifiable indignation of some of the officials would be aggravated. Also I felt that prison inmates would be aggravated. Also I felt that prison inmates would lose some faith in the committee. Those inmates felt that they had something going in the committee which would correct and improve the situation. Tonight the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) read excerpts from letters which indicated how the situations in Millhaven and perhaps other institutions were about to explode again. We have heard how there was complete quiet in the prisons while the subcommittee was meeting. Although this debate may provoke the government to do something, I felt it might exacerbate the feelings of prison inmates.
Perhaps this debate has damaged the reputation of the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais). I thought he would have known better than to attempt to oppose the motion coming from the standing committee. This resolution was supported unanimously by the committee. It came to the House in good faith. There
Concurrence in Committee Report was no partisanship showing in the desire of the standing committee to bring the entire subject before the committee in its proper sense. Yet, for some reason, the Solicitor General attempted to block it with a procedural move. I am pleased the minister reversed his position of being opposed to the motion. I gather he will support it now, but I am sure it embarrassed the government. We are at a time when the government is anxious to get legislation through, but now we are spending an entire day debating this issue. I am sure the time of the House could have been used considering some other issue. As this issue could have been handled very adequately within the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs if the opportunity were available.
In his presentation this afternoon the Solicitor General made comments concerning all the matters which have been implemented arising from the 65 recommendations of the report. I should like to refer to nine recommendations brought to my attention recently which have not been implemented. Where is the report on the inmates' rights? What about the problem of the in-House grievance and disciplinary hearings which are not as good as the minister led us to believe in his earlier comments today? The Solicitor General attempted to convince the House that the citizens' advisory committees are working effectively. We know that is not true, as I am sure he knows as well. The inmates' committees are not functioning well. I understand one of the inmates' committees in Kingston has been disbanded completely, because it was felt that it had no place or no role to play in the institution any longer. The training programs recommended in the report have not been implemented as they should have been.
The new prisons are another problem. There is room for discussion concerning the size of prisons, but obviously no adequate study has been conducted to justify the recent deci-son of the Solicitor General. The pay for work done by prisoners is grossly inadequate. The other day we learned that in some prisons there was privileged correspondence between inmates and parliamentarians openly available on charts of certain inmates for others to see. The recommendation in the report that the prison law library should be enhanced and improved has not been followed.
Today we heard some talk about partisanship. As many members have said, it is quite true there was absolutely no partisanship in the subcommittee set up to study penitentiaries. In fact, if there was any rift within that subcommittee, it was more often on an incidental basis between two members of the same party. Very rarely was there a rift between two parties. As a relatively new member of the House, it was encouraging to see that parliamentarians could work collectively toward a common goal in this case, namely, the improvement of our prisons. I was somewhat disappointed when things changed a little. This was alluded to by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. Some time last week government members of the standing committee received an updated progress report, and we were not allowed to have ours until this week.

The hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) received his copy today. One of the recommendations in which I was particularly interested was recommendation No. 62. It dealt with some changes in the administration of prisons at the local institutional level. The government undertook a research study to assess the feasibility of such an innovation. The green book indicated that two studies were done. It was concluded that it would not be a wise idea to attempt such an experiment. When we telephoned the office of the Solicitor General in an attempt to receive a copy of those two studies, we were told that they were not for publication and that we could not have them. That was not the type of co-operation which we experienced throughout the workings of the subcommittee on penitentiaries. The only reason such an excellent report was produced in the end was the perfect co-operation which existed. As other members have indicated, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville did an excellent job as committee chairman in keeping the committee non-partisan. But under the leadership of the Solicitor General, we see it falling apart.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway put her finger on the most important issue facing not only the prisons but governments in general. We have lost track entirely of the relationship which should exist between the elected representatives of the people and the people we hire on behalf of Canadians to administer and carry out the legislation we see fit to pass. There is no doubt in my mind that this is the crux of the problem.
We have heard about the failure of the CCS which I believe was in one particular area. Perhaps we have abused some of those officials in that in many cases they have attempted to implement certain recommended proposals for which we did not give them due recognition. As officials, they have assumed the role of the elected representatives. It is absolutely absurd that they have taken on the roles of policy-making and implementation.
One can look at other public institutions in the country, such as the public school system in Ontario. Its policy is formed by an elected or appointed board. Policy recommendations are passed by the board and implemented by the professionals. It is absurd that in the present system the professionals in CCS seem to think they are better judges of the needs of the country than we are. We were sent to Ottawa for the very purpose of determining what that policy should be. We made 65 recommendations, and they have turned around and told us they do not like them and are not going to put them into force. What do you think of that, Mr. Speaker?

I am quite prepared to sit down with those officials and talk with them. If they have any questions to ask, they should ask us. They come to these committee meetings and sit on one side, and they inform us in their printed report that they do not

agree with our recommendations and are not going to implement them. Why do they not come to us and say, "We see a problem in respect of recommendations Nos. 24 and 62?" They do not do that; they simply say they cannot make them work. They do not come out and say, "Perhaps we can come to some compromise in order that we can make them work." This is the attitude that is causing cynicism around this country about the parliamentary system.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has talked about how our parliamentary committee system is failing. I suggest it is failing for the same reason. We as the elected representatives are not being given proper recognition. That is due in part to the failure of the government, specifically, and in large part to the failure of this government in allowing a body of officials to run this country.

There are two recommendations about which I feel particularly concerned, namely, recommendations Nos. 24 and 62. They have reference to the management of our prisons. Strangely enough, and this substantiates my total point, those were the two recommendations of the 65 that were virtually rejected out of hand.
Recommendation No. 24 suggested a five-man board that would recommend policy to the commission. It would be responsible to the Solicitor General. The Solicitor General does not understand it. If you read what is suggested in recommendations Nos. 24 and 62, Mr. Speaker, you will have to admit that he does not understand what we are suggesting. He thinks he would be deprived of a line of authority. Obviously he does not understand the system at all, yet he comes from Ontario where this has worked beautifully in our school jurisdiction. He refuses to admit that.
The minister has been conned by this body of officials because they realize that if recommendations 24 and 62 were approved they would no longer have the power to make policy. I suggest they would be better off with the implementation of these recommendations. They would be in position to recommend policy to those who are responsible. They would have to substantiate that policy to those who are responsible for approving policy, namely, the elected representatives, who would then be prepared to accept it. I want to say something more about this attitude that is exemplified by our paid officials, particularly those in the CCS. That is an area where we have the opportunity of obser- <ng this attitude.

I should like to quote from an editorial which appeared in the Globe and Mail of February 1, 1979. It is entitled "Deregulation" and is written by Geoffrey Stevens. It hits the nail on the head and appeared, fortuitously, not long before this debate. In dealing with this problem of deregulation he has this to say:
-where does the role of the independent regulator end and the role of the accountable politician begin?
He goes on after a paragraph to state:
And there are times when the politician should step in. In an article published in the Yale Law Journal in June, 1975, two Washington legal experts, David R. Johnson and Lloyd Cutler (the latter being, coincidentally, Washington's negotiator in the Canada-U.S. fish war), argued that he should step in more often. "The necessity of delegation should not disguise the fact that whatever legitimacy inheres in agency action stems from a delegation of politically based power-
That is what I was trying to say a few minutes ago regarding those we appoint to run prisons.
The article goes on to state:
"Only elected officials can provide the requisite overview, co-ordination, and practical political judgment to weigh competing claims, make the necessary ultimate decisions, and stand accountable at the polls."
I have a beautiful excerpt here which one might think comes from a journal of recent date. It carries the headline "Sessional Papers (No. 18.)", and it is dated 1898. The portion I have here is a report from the inspector of penitentiaries, Mr. Douglas Stewart, who signs off as "Your obedient servant". It is dated, as I say, 1898. Fie is writing in the sessional papers recommending, I presume, to the Department of Justice, under the heading "General System of Control", certain things. It seems that back in 1875, over 100 years ago, the management of penitentiaries was vested in a board of directors, the very thing this subcommittee saw fit to recommend in 1977. In 1875 that board of directors was abolished and replaced by departmental control under the minister of justice.
In 1879 a commission was appointed to study penitentiaries, headed by Messrs. Tache and Miall. Mr. Stewart, the inspector of penitentiaries, had this to say:
The trend of opinion among those most closely identified with the prisons has been adverse to direct departmental control, and the case from that point of view is forcibly set out by Messrs. Tache and Miall in their report in connection with the management of the penitentiaries, dated 23rd December, 1879.
Eet me read a couple of quotations from this report of Messrs. Tache and Miall because they point out that in 1879, one hundred years ago, the very problems we are trying to correct by recommendations Nos. 24 and 62 then existed. The first quotation is as follows:
"The study of the subject of prison management, if pursued free from the influence of preconceived ideas, must lead an unbiased mind to the conviction that such institutions should be governed and directed by an organization or body of men free from political or other extraneous influences."
I would like to have another opportunity to refer to this document at a future date, Mr. Speaker. Let me conclude by saying that there is evidence to show that the system we now have did not work 100 years ago and it is not working now. It is high time we, as elected representatives, insisted that these

Concurrence in Committee Report to the service on the basis of "prime user status" under the Public Service Employment Act.
I know that the commissioner has sent to members of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs an outline of the steps taken by his service in 1978, entitled "The CCS Major Accomplishments in 1978", which runs to eight or nine pages.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-GOVERNMENT CONTRIBUTION TO HEALTH CARE PROGRAM
HEALTH AND WELFARE-GOVERNMENT CONTRIBUTION TO HEALTH CARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I drew the attention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to a problem of an increasing number of aged patients and the lack of proper chairs of medicine being established in the universities across Canada for this purpose. The over 60 years of age is the fastest growing group in our society and we have created a social and economical problem for the government with this new breed of patient with whom we have had only limited experience. Those who suffer from degenerative diseases are not cured by a pill or an antibiotic. They create new problems in medicine.
At the beginning of this century a doctor had few drugs but his presence created trust and confidence. His suggestions were indeed potent weapons, and his competence and spiritual faith carried many back from severe illness which might otherwise have proved fatal. He was often the sole comforter

in the home. Today the situation is different. This is almost a lost art. His work is now largely a hospital practice. He makes his rounds, sometimes with an army of paramedical personnel. This destroys the closeness that existed when the doctor, the patient and the family were the only ones concerned.
Let us take a look at the beginning of this century when life expectancy was just over 40 years. Today life expectancy is just over 75 years. In the over 75-year age group the average woman lives 5 years longer than a man. In the over 85-year age group there are two women to every man. With the advent of scientific medicine at the beginning of the century life expectancy increased.
In 1900 there were many diseases. The first medicine we discovered of any real concern which made an impact on the world's scientific field was smallpox vaccine. Along with that was the development of antiseptic surgery by Dr. Lister. At the beginning of this century there was recognition that typhoid fever was caused by an organism. This organism was found in the environment and in polluted drinking water or food that was handled by someone with the organism. It would have been impossible to have fought the First World War if we had not discovered the cause and prevention of typhoid fever.
Then we come to the scientific era of antitoxin and diphtheria. This disease was one of the great killers in 1905. I remember a family of five who lived next door to me who died from diphtheria. An antitoxin had been used in the first case discovered in the neighbourhood but it had been used in too small a dose. Quickly followed by the diphtheria and scarlet fever antitoxin was a whole host of disease preventives. Next came the discovery of insulin for the treatment of diabetes, by Drs. Banting and Best. As a result of this a number of young lives were saved. I remember a Dr. Gilchrist, a childhood diabetic, who later became a famous doctor in Toronto. I could give many more examples, including the treatment of pernicious anemia.
Following that came the sulphur drugs and antibiotics, with the advent of penicillin and the golden age of aureomycin followed by the tetracyclines etc. Then all at once we found that infections were not the biggest killer of people up to the age of 35 or 40, instead today accidents take more lives.
Then we found some people approaching the age of 50 were developing chronic diseases. These diseases included those of the heart, the lungs, the arteries, the cardiovascular system, rheumatoid arthritis, emphysema, and so on. Sometimes people were not just afflicted with one ailment but two. We found out that by comparing a person aged 60 with a person aged 20 or 30, the 60-year-old would have three times the number of illnesses. As a result of many postmortems performed on people in their nineties it has been found that not only do these people have one disease but sometimes three or four, and perhaps as many as one to three cancers in their vital organs. It was found too that the cancer had not always been the cause of death.
February 6, 1979

This field has never been explored fully because all at once it is ongoing. Ten years ago we were told this field would be opened up, but nothing has been done yet. The geriatric specialty is not taught in this country, and I want to give you a brief illustration of that. Very few physicians have special training in the complexities and the needs of the aged patient. Older people very often manifest symptoms entirely different from those commonly associated with certain ailments among those less advanced in years. Many diseases occur to me in this context, but I shall not refer to them now. A fellow who is 80 can show symptoms quite different from those which would be expected in the case of a younger man like yourself, Mr. Speaker.
The place to generate the new training which is required has to be our medical schools. And listen to this-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will begin by commending the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) for his persistence in bringing up this whole question of the need for geriatric care. He speaks with knowledge, interest and enthusiasm, and he will probably continue to do the same in the future. He is a doctor and a senior citizen, an expert on this topic, so it is good to hear from him this evening.
On December 14, 1978, the hon. member drew the attention of the House to the changing health requirements of an aging population. The shift in composition of the Canadian population is a major consideration of health planners at all levels of government and in the health professions. A number of issues related to these changes were raised at a national symposium on aging held in Ottawa in October, 1978.
Demographic forecasting is very complex, and trends may be altered considerably over the course of several decades. Nevertheless, there is considerable agreement among experts that the proportion of the population aged 65 years and over is likely to rise from the 1976 level of 8.7 per cent to about 12 per cent by the turn of the century. One need not be overwhelmed by this transition; Great Britain, France, Austria, East Germany and Sweden are among countries with 12 per cent or more of their population over 65 years of age.
Planning for the future does not only involve services for senior citizens. All segments of the population are affected by demographic transition, and comprehensive planning is needed. The provinces, of course, have direct responsibility for provision of most health and welfare services. Several provinces have initiated programs for adjusting their services to the needs of a changing population. The increased flexibility in provincial use of federal funds provided under the new financing arrangements assists them in making these modifications.
In response to suggestions from a number of provincial and voluntary agencies, a bureau on aging has recently been
Adjournment Debate
established in my department. This bureau will serve as a communications link between the federal government, provincial governments and organizations for the aged, and will become a contact point for individuals and senior citizens' organizations.
The health of senior citizens is not determined solely by the availability of "geriatric medicine". An objective of the department is the promotion of a healthful lifestyle and an increased sense of personal responsibility for one's physical condition. Prevention of damage to our health at earlier stages of life may have a profound effect on our state of health and well-being as we grow older.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRO RATA PENSIONS FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRO RATA PENSIONS FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 5 I raised a question in the House with regard to pro rata pensions for widows of disabled veterans. As the legislation now stands, widows of veterans receiving less than 48 per cent disability pension are left without a pension. I also asked whether the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) would tell the House when he plans to bring in pro rata pensions for these women, thereby implementing a recommendation of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The Deputy Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the provision of the Pension Act upon which the hon. member bases his question. However, I have not had a chance to talk with the Minister of Veterans Affairs about this. I will draw the question to his attention. I am sure he will give it his usual sympathetic consideration.
I then asked the Deputy Prime Minister whether he would promise to bring forward legislation dealing with the recommendations in whole or in part before an election is called. He answered:
-I cannot guarantee that legislation will be brought forward during the present session. In the normal course, the minister involved makes a recommendation to cabinet on these matters. Until that recommendation is made, such reports are not normally studied by cabinet.
The question here is why the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) did not raise this matter in cabinet. It seems very strange that a recommendation which was made in 1975 by the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs has not even been raised in cabinet by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The recommendation was as follows:
Your committee also recommends to the House that consideration be given to amending the Pension Act to provide that a widow's pension be awarded on a sliding scale as follows:
When at the time of death of the prisoner he was, or would have been in receipt of a pension assessed at 47 per cent or less, that pension be paid to the widow in double proportion to the assessed degree of the pensioner's disability as it relates to the basic pension granted to widows.
That was the basic proposal, and now, three and a half years later, we learn from the Deputy Prime Minister that the Minister of Veterans Affairs has not even raised this matter for consideration in cabinet. That is unbelievable.

February 6, 1979
Adjournment Debate
That brings us to the question of priorities. It was announced just last week that the government has found SI8 million to build hockey arenas across the country. Hockey arenas have a higher priority than finding money for the widows of veterans. That is a strange priority.
It seems to me that bribing the Canadian people with hockey arenas just before an election is just a gimmick, and it should not be a higher priority than the widows of veterans. We also found out just last week that the government has found money so that Statistics Canada can conduct a study on the amount of toilet paper and the number of sanitary pads female members of a houselhold use. Those are the strange priorities of this government. It conducts studies on what people do in their bathrooms, but it cannot raise money for the widows of veterans. We will be passing this information around the nation, and to all widows and veterans' organizations, in order to point out this government's priorities. Its priorities are toilet paper, sanitary napkins, and bribing voters with hockey arenas.
Another recommendation which has not been fulfilled dates back to 1970 and deals with the basic rate of disability pension. As a result of the work of the committee to survey the organization and work of the Canadian Pension Commission- that was the Woods commission-the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs recommended to the House of Commons in June of 1970 that the basic rate of the 100 per cent disability pension should be the same as the average or composite wage of five categories of unskilled employees in the public service, and that subsequent increases in the pension should be based on the same formula.
Obviously, the Minister of Veterans Affairs has not discussed this in cabinet either. A junior minister just appointed to the cabinet recently makes more headway than the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who has been in the cabinet since 1972. The Minister of Veterans Affairs has not raised these matters.
There are other matters we had hoped the minister would raise, but apparently he has not. One of those matters is compensation for prisoners of war over and above the disability pension. Another recommendation the committee made is that the government ensure that disability pension increases are not accompanied by reductions in other awards or allowances. [DOT]
I would suggest that the government take a second look at its priorities. With the uncontrolled inflation which exists in this country and the problems that our senior citizens are having, this is not the time for squandering money on the useless statistics that Canada studies. It is time they looked at our veterans affairs problems. I hope we will have a straightforward answer from the parliamentary secretary tonight, some assurance that legislation will be brought in, before an election is called, to deal with widows' pensions, because if it is not brought in before an election, six or eight months could elapse before the next Conservative government could deal

with these problems. Now is the time to deal with them, not six or eight months from now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilbert Parent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PRO RATA PENSIONS FOR WIDOWS OF DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for bringing his question forward. I discussed the matter with the minister, and I am pleased to bring the information that the question of providing pro rata pensions for widows of veterans who had been in receipt of disability pensions at a rate less than 48 per cent is being currently studied. At present if a veteran's pension has been assessed at the rate of 48 per cent or more, his surviving dependants would be pensionable. It should be remembered that, in addition, a widow will be pensioned if her husband's death occurred during war time or was attributable to service, regardless of the degree of the assessment of disability.
All veterans' benefits undergo constant review to see what changes can be made to improve their lot and that of their dependants, and I assure the hon. member that the government considers their well-being as a priority.

Mr. Speaker, while my remarks tonight are being addressed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde), I should like to point out that he is the third minister of justice since I first introduced this subject more than two years ago. On October 29, 1976, I asked the then minister of justice during the question period what response, if any, he had made to representations from a number of Canadian municipalities asking for federal assistance in combating the rising wave of vandalism throughout the country.
I became concerned when I learned that the Minister of Justice had not made any effort to follow up on these requests, especially those from Ontario municipalities led by the town council of Trenton, Ontario. The Trenton council, and the councils of other municipalities across the province, felt that the problem was serious enough to warrant a combined federal-provincial assault on this senseless crime. So far as I can determine, neither of the two previous justice ministers has even expressed an interest in following through on these requests. They both answered my questions in much the same way, namely, that vandalism is purely a provincial matter and that any initiatives concerning federal-provincial co-operation in this matter must come from the provincial attorneys general. I reject that argument on both counts.
The answers given by the minister lead me to believe that they have failed utterly to get the point I have been trying to make over the past two years. In the first place, the minister admitted that vandalism is covered by the Criminal Code, which is the federal body of law. But the Criminal Code is administered jointly by the Minister of Justice and the several provincial attorneys general. In the second place, the initiative for establishing a joint federal-provincial effort to combat vandalism could come from the federal Minister of Justice as well as from the provincial attorneys general.
February 6, 1979

What the two previous justice ministers failed to understand is that much of the vandalism of which I speak is directed against federal institutions, such as post offices. In some areas of the country, post offices have become favourite targets of vandals. While the federal government is responsible for apprehending and prosecuting in these cases, it does not do so in isolation from the provincial agencies and departments.
Apart from the senseless nature of vandalism and the appalling cost to the law-abiding public, there is another good reason why the federal Minister of Justice should be interested in mounting an effective campaign against vandalism in cooperation with the provinces.
The opinion widely held today among law enforcement and social agencies is that vandalism is more than just a senseless crime against private and public property. It is believed that vandalism is a step along the way to more serious crimes such as muggings, assaults, robberies, rapes and others. The nature of vandalism itself indicates a serious lack of respect for the law and for the rights and property of law-abiding citizens. When vandals operate undetected or when they get a slap on the wrist instead of a deterrent sentence when they appear before the courts, they become bolder, and the logical progression is into more serious types of crimes. Our only protection against this senseless and costly criminal behaviour is a more vigorous pursuit of vandals and stiffer penalties when they are apprehended and convicted. These are just some of the reasons why I believe it is imperative that the federal government get into the act through the office of the Minister of Justice.
The Minister of Justice should initiate contacts with provincial attorneys general to see if there is any real interest on their part in a federal-provincial assault on vandalism. A higher success rate in apprehending vandals would do much to convince such people that they are in a very real danger of being caught and convicted, which should reduce the incidence of such crime. In any case, serious contacts between the pertinent federal and provincial authorities could have some beneficial results. Surely it is worth some effort on their part to serve notice on vandals that their days are numbered.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude-Andre Lachance (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Vandalism does not exist as such in the Criminal Code. What is generally called vandalism is provided for under the sections of the Criminal Code dealing with mischief, section 387, and the wilful damage of property when the alleged amount of damage does not exceed S50, section 388. Mischief is one of those offences where the prosecution can proceed by way of indictment or summary conviction.
If the prosecution proceeds by way of indictment, there are three possible sentences. When the mischief causes actual danger to human health, the accused is liable to imprisonment for life. If the mischief is in relation to public property, the maximum punishment is 14 years. Finally, if the offence is in
Adjournment Debate
relation to private property, the accused is liable to imprisonment for five years.
In all cases of mischief, whether in relation to public property or private property, the prosecution can choose to proceed by way of summary conviction, and in that case, the maximum punishment is imprisonment for six months, a fine of $500 or both. Damage under $50 caused to property is an offence punishable on summary conviction, and there again the maximum punishment is imprisonment for six months, a fine of $500 or both.
It should be noted that those punishments are a maximum. The courts very rarely impose the maximum punishment. They rather use other forms of sentences available to deal with each case individually. Those other forms of sentences are conditional or unconditional paroles, fines, suspended sentences and probation.
If the court decides to impose a period of probation it can include in the terms of that probation a proviso that the accused will have to make restitution or reparation to any person aggrieved or injured by the commission of the infraction. And if the accused wilfully omits to comply with one of the terms of the probation he is liable to be charged with a summary offence and punished for such a violation. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1978 introduces in our criminal law new types of sentences, such as the community service orders provided in Bill C-21. Moreover, this bill provides for compensation and restitution. Under these new provisions, the court must assess each case to ensure that it can make an order of compensation or restitution without placing the accused under a probation order.
According to the terms of our constitution, the role of the federal parliament is restricted to establishing criminal law. Parliament has attacked squarely the issue of vandalism by including criminal misdeeds in the Criminal Code and providing sentences of five and 14 years of imprisonment and life imprisonment for this offence. The courts have all the necessary freedom of action under the present provisions to use their discretionary powers. Increasing the provided penalty would be like trying to kill a fly with a cannon and the courts would simply not impose the new sentences provided.
It is extremely difficult to imagine a particular case of vandalism against private property which would justify a sentence of more than five years in prison. The administration of justice in a province is under strict provincial jurisdiction. If vandalism is a problem in a particular area, the Criminal Code gives the substitute of the attorney general all the flexibility required to solve the problem. He can use an indictment rather than a summary conviction. Moreover, once the guilt of the accused has been proven, he can suggest a prison term to the court rather than a fine or a suspended sentence.

February 6, 1979
Adjournment Debate
Finally, the provincial attorney general can appeal the sentence to the appeals court if he finds it insufficient and fears that it does not constitute an acceptable precedent as a sentence for a misdeed. I wish to thank the hon. member for having brought up this question.
